reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: This study from Notti and colleagues provides structural insights into the inter-subunit conformational relationships that can be assumed in the extracellular and transmembrane domains within TCR-CD3 complexes when solubilized in detergent, or when embedded within artificial membranes after reconstitution within nanodiscs. It makes important additions to the growing library of available cryoEM structures of TCR-CD3 complexes by providing examples embedded within membranes, which are expected to be more physiological than detergent solubilized complexes. Unlike prior detergent-soluble structures, showing the ectodomain of the TCR situated more upright relative to the CD3 heterodimers, the two nanodisc-embedded structures (NDI and NDII) adopt more closed arrangements with the TCR variable regions nearly touching the tops of the CD3 heterodimers. In contrast, nanodisc-embedded TCR-CD3 bound to pHLA adopt a more extended open structure in the ectodomain. The juxtamembrane connecting peptides in the extracellular space, as well as the transmembrane domains of the subunits, also show changes in the unliganded NDI/II conformations relative to the liganded states. Notably, the transmembrane regions of the subunits adopt a splayed relationship in the unliganded state that straightens in the liganded structures, consistent with prior functional data. The authors conclude that the more compact NDI and NDII complexes represent the resting state whereas the open configuration represents a liganded signaling conformation, with changes in the orientation of the constituent subunits in the ectodomain, extracellular juxtamembrane connecting peptides, and transmembrane domains providing a mechanism by which pMHC engagement leads to signaling across the membrane. Experimentally, the study relies largely on cryoEM with some supporting biochemical and functional data: 1. The investigators have the required expertise for the study. The structures appear to be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures. a. The lack of order in some regions creates some problems for insights into allosteric changes for NDI and NDII. 2. The methods indicate that different combinations of constructs were used to purify the TCR-CD3 complexes incorporated into nanodiscs for determination of unliganded structures in NDI and ND2 than were used for the liganded complexes. a. While unlikely, it is formally possible that changes in subunit tags, be they HIS or EGFP or 2A tags left on the subunits, could differentially impact the spatial relationship of the subunits within assembled complexes. What motivated the change in approach is unclear but this caveat should be noted. i. Determination of the structures of the unliganded complexes within the same preparation from which particles were picked and refined for determination of the liganded structures would address this caveat and lend confidence to the approach. The expectation is that the unliganded particles would assume the more closed orientation. ii. Providing the complex construct sequences in the supplemental information would be beneficial to the field. 3. The methods would benefit from better referencing and description of the TCR-HLA paired used and the choice thereof. 4. The manuscript would benefit from an explanation as to why, for the liganded structures, the investigators are confident that the ND-embedded complexes underwent an allosteric change from NDI or NDII. Is there a chance that a subset of complexes existed in an open conformation that favored binding, and that the process of picking and refining particles preferentially enriched liganded particle? 5. The biochemical and functional experiments are performed by conventional techniques, are well-controlled, and are reasonably well-presented for interpretation but they do not add much to the study. a. One caveat is that there is no indication that the disulphide blots or functional assays were performed more than once to ensure reproducibility. b. The methods do not indicate the temperature at which the functional assays were performed (presumably 37ºC). i. This detail is important to ensure others in the field could reproduce the work. c. It would aid in evaluation to add the molecular weights to the blots in Sup Fig 5 rather than color coding the marker and requiring the reader to cross reference the figure legend each time. d. The full gel for Sup Fig 5d and 5e would be helpful for evaluating the extent to which mature complexes are enriched through purification. The zeta subunits are below the cropping of the gel. e. The conclusions regarding Fig 7i and 7j are questionable given the data. i. The histograms in Fig 7i clearly show lower expression of the S104C/V182C mutant than the WT (note that the x-axis is on a log scale). The difference in tetramer staining, as well as the difference in signaling in Fig 7j, could easily be due to differences in surface expression of the WT and mutant TCRs. ii. I recommend removing these data as they do not add to the study and could be misinterpreted. iii. For these data to be convincing, the investigators would need to make multiple independently generated sets of Jurkat lines with matched TCR expression and show that they consistently produced functional differences between the WT and Mut. iv. The investigators should also show that the disulphide bonds are formed on TCR-CD3 complexes that have translocated to the cell surface. Title, Abstract, and Discussion level conclusions: 6. The structures provided herein are interesting and make an important contribution to the field. They provide strong evidence that different inter-subunit conformational relationships can be adopted by the transmembrane and connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3 complex subunits. That alone is important information for the field. 7. The title and abstract level conclusions cannot fully be substantiated by the data and should be calibrated to better reflect the limitations of the data. a. The conclusion that the more closed NDI/II structures represent the resting state are one of several plausible interpretations of the data. As the authors note, the T cell membrane has variable subdomains with different lipid compositions, and it is unclear if porcine neuron membranes are analogous to the membrane subdomain inhabited by TCR-CD3 complexes on the T cell membrane. b. Different environments will have different membrane curvatures (e.g., during transport to the cell membrane or when localized at the tip of a filapodia). Given that the complex is membrane-anchored during assembly and transport to the cell surface, the different conformations may represent assembly or vesicular transport conformations necessitated by the nature of those membrane. c. The effort to present functional data in Fig 7 to support their conclusions is not convincing for the reasons outlined above. These data should be removed. 8. The Discussion level conclusion “…that intrinsic conformational change in the TCR-CD3 is necessary for early TCR-CD3 activation” is not fully substantiated by the data for the reasons outlined above. However, discussing the structures presented here within the context of biochemical and functional data from other studies that support their interpretation would allow the authors to offer a plausible molecular mechanism for those prior observations and lend confidence to the author’s contention that intrinsic changes within the complex occur in the absence of intracellular kinase signaling. a. In addition to the paper cited by the authors (PMID: 34260912), it would be relevant to discuss studies showing exposure of cytoplasmic juxtamembrane proline rich sequence on CD3e can occur in the absence of kinase signaling (even at 4ºC) (PMID: 12110186, 15728235). b. Data that more directly complements the ligand-induced transmembrane allosteric changes observed here, and which should also be noted for completeness, comes from a study indicating that the zeta transmembrane domains are splayed in TCR-CD3 in the resting state and move together in the liganded state in the absence of intracellular signaling (PMID: 26231119). 9. The discussion regarding the potential role of glycosylation in regulating signaling is interesting. a. There is evidence for regulation of gdTCR-CD3 through differential glycosylation that may be worth considering (PMID: 12438426). 10. Evidence that TCR-CD3 inhabits specific membrane sub-domains that concatenate with other distinct sub-domains (e.g., LAT containing domains) are worth consideration (PMID: 20010844). If distinct membrane sub-domains have distinct thicknesses and composition, this could force changes in intra- and inter-subunit transmembrane orientations. They could also exchange sterols at the subdomain interface. They could also potentially impact lipid-protein interactions at the conserved patches noted on CD3. Regarding novelty, extensibility, broad interest and overall impact: 11. This study highlights the value of determining the structures of multi-subunit complex in the membrane environment . a. Doing so for the TCR-CD3 complex is highly novel. 12. This study provides key evidence that inter-subunit allosteric changes in the transmembrane and juxtamembrane extracellular connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3 complex can occur upon ligand engagement. a. This finding is not novel in the broad sense that evidence already exists for allosteric changes in TCR-CD3 upon ligand engagement in the absence of other signaling events, as noted above; nevertheless, it offers important molecular insights into how these changes could occur. b. A key strength of this study, for which it should make an important impact on the field, is therefore derived from contributing to a growing body of evidence that such conformational changes are the earliest events in TCR-CD3 signaling upon engagement of cognate ligands. 13. This study is likely to be of broad interests to people who study multi-subunit signaling receptors, lymphocyte activation, and receptor biology more broadly. 14. This study will also be of impact for its extensibility. The author’s present many key findings that are idea generating, and these ideas are worth testing to work towards a better understanding of this complex.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Notti et al. Response to Reviewer Comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Over the past few decades, many studies have elucidated structural data regarding the
TCR–CD3 complex in both unbound and ligand-bound states. However, the mechanism
through which ligand binding to the extracellular domains induces TCR conformational
change and activation remains enigmatic. In this manuscript, Notti and colleagues seek
to address this important question by employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
They present the structures of the unliganded TCR–CD3 complex in detergent micelles
and nanodiscs, along with the HLA-bound human TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs.
This study identifies two previously unobserved conformations of the unliganded TCR–
CD3 complex in nanodiscs, termed “closed and compacted” conformations. Notably,
these appear distinct from the “open and extended” conformations reported in detergent
environments. Cross-linking data seem to corroborate the idea that these conformations
represent the resting state of an unstimulated TCR–CD3 complex on T cells.
Furthermore, the structure of the nanodisc-embedded TCR–CD3 complex bound to
HLA showcases significant conformational changes upon ligand binding, adopting an
“open and extended” conformation.
My major concerns are regarding the map quality of the “closed and compacted”
conformations, which exhibit significant preferred orientation that could substantially
impact the structural model. Given the authors’ aim to discuss the conformational
differences between the resting and activated states, these issues are particularly
relevant.
1. The ND-I and ND-II maps appear abnormal (Supplementary Figs. 2c, d), which is
also indicated by the 3D FSC analyses of these maps (Supplementary Figs. 2f, h).
These analyses suggest severe preferred orientation, with missing orientations parallel
to the cell membrane. A representative 2D classification image should be included for
further evaluation.
Authors’ response:
We thank the referee for reviewing the maps and models. As we described in main text
lines 121-128 and showed in Supplementary Fig. 2f,h, preferred particle orientation and
its effect on 3D reconstruction (i.e., map anisotropy) likely impacted reconstruction
quality, alongside other factors like conformational dynamism. However, efforts to
ameliorate particle orientation preference with graphene oxide grids or fluorinated
detergents did not improve map quality (lines 125-126). Examination of 2D classes for
the nanodisc dataset do show a preference for “top” (membrane normal) views, but
views off this axis are also seen, including views orthogonal or near-orthogonal to the
top view. These data are now included as Supplementary Fig. 2i. Comparison of these
“(tilted)-side” views with those from the GDN dataset (Supplementary Fig. 2j) clearly
show differences corresponding to opening-closing and extension-compaction.
Reviewer #1:
2. The authors claim that much of the density in the ND-I and ND-II maps has an
estimated local resolution better than 4 Å, asserting that the maps are of sufficient
quality to build models. However, more representative local density maps with the
corresponding models are needed to validate this claim. In fact, the deposited model
does not satisfactorily match the deposited map.
Authors’ response:
We refer the reviewer to Supplementary Fig. 3, where the fit of the models to
DeepEMhancer-sharpened maps is shown at the level of whole-density slices (panels c-
e) and zoomed in to areas of interest with specific features serving as intrinsic fiducial
markers across maps (panels f-h). Additional sections through the density maps with
the corresponding models have been added as requested (Supplementary Fig. 3i-k).
We also refer the reviewer to Supplementary Table 2, where model validation statistics
are shown, and highlight that holistic metrics of model quality (e.g., Molprobity score)
and fit (e.g., dFSCmodel) at the standard 0.143 cutoff are in general agreement with (or
in some cases exceed) the nominal resolutions.
To be as transparent and reproducible as possible, we chose the raw,
unsharpened maps to serve as the “primary” maps in the PDB/EMDB, because we
conservatively performed all statistical analyses of map-to-model correlation using these
maps. However, we did also deposit standard global B-factor-sharpened and
DeepEMhancer-sharpened maps in the unified PDB/EMDB deposition system, and
these maps can be accessed in the EMDB (Additional maps 1 and 2 under the
“Additional data” tab for each dataset). For ease of review, we are also uploading all
sharpened maps and the corresponding models to Figshare. We recommend the use of
these sharpened maps for visual inspection, as is standard in single-particle cryo-EM
(see also Methods section, lines 879-888 for a description of map assessment and post
processing). We do note the assessment of reviewer #5, that “[t]he structures appear to
be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that
could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures.”
Lastly, the effect of conformational dynamics on local map quality and its
functional implications merits brief discussion. The local resolution maps for ND-I and
ND-II are consistent with specific regions of disorder and other regions that are well
ordered, suggesting significant conformational dynamics. This interpretation is
consistent with the observation of more than one conformational state (ND-I and ND-II)
within this dataset. The ordering of previously disordered or poorly ordered domains
upon ligand binding is consistent with prior studies showing that ligand binding induces
TCR rigidification (see main text lines 346-351) and suggests that these disorder-to-
order transitions are functionally important. Moreover, the in vivo crosslinking data
presented here (and that of the Krogsgaard group, discussed below) provide support for
the nanodisc conformations as the true physiologic resting state for the TCR.
Taken together, we interpret our ND-I and ND-II maps not as “abnormal,” but as more
biologically accurate reflections of the TCR–CD3’s dynamic resting conformation, which
is reflected in areas of lower local resolution in these maps.
Reviewer #1:
3. It is important to note that preferred orientation may also lead to the density of
cholesterol molecules clustering together.
Authors’ response:
While map anisotropy might cause “smearing” or “stretching” of the density along axes
perpendicular to missing views, this would not affect solely the density attributed to
cholesterol, and well-ordered regions of the sharpened maps (e.g., ectodomain
immunoglobulin folds) do not suggest a global compression of the reconstruction along
the membrane-normal axis to cause artifactual clustering of the cholesterol density in
the map.
Reviewer #1:
4. Have the authors considered using graphene oxide or some other detergents to
improve preferred orientations? Alternatively, tilting the sample stage could be an
effective approach.
Authors’ response:
Please see main text lines 125-126 for discussion of these efforts. We note also that
DeepEMhancer post-processing has been shown to reduce map anisotropy (Sanchez-
Garcia et al., 2024, PMID: 38612769), which may in part explain the improvement in
map interpretability with application of this post-processing strategy. We have also
tested a recently developed deconvolution-based algorithm for reduction of map
anisotropy (AR-Decon; Li et al., 2025; PMID: 40060637), but this algorithm did not
improve map interpretability or map-to-model correlation, nor did it meaningfully change
the models built from the maps. Indeed, the RMSD between models refined on the
unsharpened maps and the AR-Decon-processed maps were less than 1 Å. As there
are no discernible changes in the models, we do not include these data.
Reviewer #1:
Overall, while the manuscript presents intriguing findings, addressing these concerns
regarding map quality and model validation is essential for supporting the authors’
conclusions.
Authors’ response:
See comments above.

Major concerns:
1) An important concern is the physiological relevance of the 2 nanodiscs-based
‘closed’ conformations. There is a concern that the 2 conformations are not due to
heterogeneity arising from reconstituting the αβTCR-CD3 complex in nanodiscs. A
recent study by Dalal et al., Nature Commun., 2024 found that reconstituting pentameric
ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC) in different nanodiscs produces distinct structures by
cryo-EM. The study also suggested the use of larger nanodiscs mimics lipid membrane
environment better. Based on this, did the authors try different nanodiscs based on size
to select the best environment to study the αβTCR-CD3 complex? If so, these results
should be discussed.
Authors’ response:
When reconstituting an integral membrane protein in lipid nanodiscs, it is important to
ensure that the MSP size (and thus nanodisc diameter) is sufficient to allow for
incorporation of the membrane with a buffer layer of lipids to minimize obligate MSP-
target protein interactions. The most likely explanation for the different structures
observed for pLGIC in different nanodiscs is that some of the nanodiscs used were too
small in this regard (Hiotis et al., 2025; PMID: 40203538). However, for single-particle
cryo-EM of relatively small membrane protein complexes like the TCR–CD3, it is
necessary to use the smallest possible nanodisc to facilitate particle alignment on
ordered protein density (and not MSP/lipid amorphous density). In this work, we used
the MSP1D1ΔH5 nanodisc system. The referee seems to question whether this
nanodisc might introduce artifacts by being too small for the system of interest. If this
nanodisc were too small, we would expect the TCR to favor an open/extended
conformation, by virtue of insufficient lipid-protein interaction area to promote
compaction and by favoring the smaller TM cross-sectional profile of this “less splayed”
conformation. That is to say, we would expect an inadequately sized nanodisc to
generate an artifactually open/extended TCR–CD3, not to induce the novel
conformations we report here. Nonetheless, prior to pursuing single-particle cryo-EM,
we did simulate the incorporation of the open/extended conformation of the TCR–CD3
(PDB 6JXR at the time) into various sized nanodiscs using the CharmmGUI molecular
dynamics preparation interface. This approach reassured us that the MSP1D1ΔH5
nanodisc ( ~8nm diameter) would have adequate cross-sectional area to incorporate the
only known conformation of the TCR–CD3 at that time with a buffer of lipids between
target protein and MSP. We show these data in Supplementary Fig. 2k-m, and briefly
discuss this in main text lines 117-120.
Reviewer #2:
2) There’s a recent study by Natarajan et al., EMBO Rep., 2024 that studied the in situ
cell-surface conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex using photo-crosslinkers. This
study determined that there were no significant differences between the cell surface and
detergent-purified conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. Further, they identified that
there were no large conformational changes in the αβTCR-CD3 structure in the
presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. The study, based on information from the
current manuscript, attempted to detect changes in crosslinks between TCRα-CD3δ
region in the presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. However, they couldn’t infer
any conformational changes occurring in this region based on their evidence. The
Natarajan et al. study needs to be extensively discussed in the manuscript especially
since it was conducted on mammalian cells which is much more physiologically relevant
than detergents or nanodiscs.
Authors’ response:
We thank the referees for encouraging discussion of this recent work from Michelle
Krogsgaard’s group, which was published during revisions of this manuscript. We make
several points in response to their assessment, and as requested, discuss their findings
extensively in the main text (lines 441-497).
First, we point out that our engineered disulfide crosslinking studies of the human
1G4 TCR (Figure 5) and functional studies in T cells (Figure 7) were indeed performed
in human cells. Natarajan et al. studied the heterologous expression of mouse 2B4 TCR
in human cells, and while the impact of this mismatch on a nuanced understanding of
TCR conformational dynamics is uncertain, our studies of a human TCR in human cells
are at least as physiologically relevant.
Nonetheless, we find that our novel resting state structures are in remarkable
agreement with the data of Natarajan et al., explaining nearly all of their crosslinking
findings for the unliganded TCR–CD3 in situ that they could not explain with the
structures of the TCR–CD3 in detergent. For example, Natarajan et al. report an
unexpected crosslink between the mouse TCRβ CC’ loop residues S170 and G171
(human S186 and G187) and CD3δ. In our models, compaction of the TCR–CD3 in
conformation ND-I brings CD3δ residues 26-30 in closer proximity to TCRβ residues
186 and 187 than the GDN conformation (red arrows, Supplementary Fig. 9a), making
crosslinking plausible. Similarly, Natarajan et al. report crosslinks between the TCRβ
FG-loop and CD3γ, which would not be predicted by the conformation of the TCR–CD3
in detergent (Supplementary Fig. 9b, right). However, closure and compaction in ND-I
bring the FG-loop into close proximity with the CD3γ amino terminus (Supplementary
Fig. 9b, left, dashed circle). Lastly, they report crosslinks between the helix 4–F-strand
region of TCRβ and CD3ϵ and CD3δ, which they wrote could not be explained by the
structure of the TCR–CD3 in detergent. The mouse TCRβ R207 (human R223)
crosslink to CD3ϵ is indeed incompatible with the GDN conformation (Supplementary
Fig. 9c, right), but this residue is brought into close proximity of CD3ϵ in the ND-I
conformation (Supplementary Fig. 9c, left). In contrast to their assessment, the mouse
TCRβ F202 (human F218) crosslink to CD3δ is compatible with both the open/extended
and ND-II closed/compacted conformations that we report (Supplementary Fig. 9d).
Taken together, the photo-crosslinking data reported by Natarajan et al. provide strong
in vivo support for our novel, closed/compacted resting conformation for the TCR–CD3
complex.
Natarajan et al. went on to analyze the effect of activating ligands (pMHC
tetramers and activating antibodies) on TCR–CD3 conformation using their photo-
crosslinking assay. However, we contend that this analysis was flawed in the following
ways and cannot exclude the possibility of ligand-induced conformational change:
1. Most p-azido phenylalanine substitution sites used in this study would not be
expected to show changes in subunit-level crosslinking pattern on ligand-induced
receptor activation. In Figure 6a of their report, Natarajan et al. schematize the
sites selected for crosslinking readout with and without activating ligands. Most of
these sites (exceptions discussed below) are at the core interfaces between the
CD3 ectodomains and/or the TCR constant domains. Our models do not suggest
that there are gross structural changes at these interfaces, and thus we would
not predict changes in crosslinking readout from these mutants.
2. We might have hypothesized that changes in the FG-loop-directed crosslinks
would be observed on ligand binding (TCRβ E221, W225 in their study).
However, the only ligand used to stimulate the receptor for these mutants was
the FG-loop-binding H57 antibody, and by our read of the report, it is not
apparent that binding of the antibody to the mutants was assessed. For example,
the side chain of W225 stabilizes the fold of the FG-loop, forming the
hydrophobic core of this microdomain. Mutation of this residue would be
reasonably expected to affect H57 binding. Lastly, without quantitation, it is
difficult to assess whether the reporters are not in fact showing any changes in
crosslinking efficiency.
3. Natarajan et al. directly assessed crosslinks based on our reported TCRα and
CD3δ interface and their crosslink-based computational models. One crosslink
designed from each of these structural hypotheses was expressed on the cell
surface. The reporter based on our cryo-EM models formed a crosslink between
TCRα and CD3δ (see their Appendix Fig. 16c) and the reporter based on their
open/extended model did not form a crosslink. As with the other crosslinking data
discussed above, this finding actually supports our novel resting state
conformations.
4. They show that qualitatively, this crosslink (human CD3δ D77 p-Aza to TCRα)
persists after activating ligand exposure. However, this is what we would expect
given the low structural resolution and nonspecificity of the photocrosslinking
approach. That is to say, the crosslinking readout in their report is unidirectionally
specific: while the p-azido phenylalanine mutation site is specified, the site of
crosslinking on the target polypeptide is not. A complex in two different
conformations for which the photocrosslinker remains in close proximity to the
target polypeptide chain (even in proximity of totally different target residues) will
still show a crosslink-induced gel shift on Western blot by this assay. For both of
our open/extended conformations (GDN and ND-HLA), the D77 Cβ remains 8-9
Å from TCRα (Supplementary Fig. 9e). This distance is comparable to the 9-10 Å
radius previously used by the Krogsgaard group as a cutoff for plausible
crosslinking (Wang et al., 2014; PMID: 25061810). Modeling the UV-activated
nitrene intermediate of CD3δ D77 p-azido phenylalanine into ND-HLA as the
most likely rotamer of tyrosine places the reactive nitrene less than 4 Å from the
TCRα backbone (Supplementary Fig. 9e).
3) In the result section ‘The unliganded TCR-CD3 is closed and compacted in vivo’,
multiple cysteine mutants were created to establish disulfide linkages which were tested
by SDS-PAGE analyses and Western blotting. However, these mutants must be tested
for viability by using pMHC tetramers and compared to the wild type. In Figure 7,
S104C/V182C mutant is tested for NY-ESO-1-MHC-tetramer binding. Similarly, all
mutants generated should be tested for its viability.
Authors’ response:
The hypothesis being tested by these crosslinking experiments was structural, not
functional. HLA binding is not germane to the question here, which is strictly whether
the residues are present within a specified radius of one another. We make no assertion
of the HLA-binding competence of these mutants, with the exception of that used for
functional analyses (TCRα S104C/V182C).
Reviewer #2:
In the same experiment, Western blot analyses were done for identifying disulfide
linkages between TCRα and CD3δ. However, the blots were stained only for EGFP
which is conjugated with TCRβ. To rule out any artifacts, a construct containing a tag
should be conjugated to CD3δ to aid in CD3δ-TCRαβ crosslinks detection like the one
used in Natarajan et al., EMBO Rep., 2024.
Authors’ response:
It is not clear what specific artifacts are hypothesized by the referee. For each of the
mutants at the TCRα-CD3δ interface in Figure 5, a control is shown in which the mutant
is paired with wild-type TCRα or CD3δ to rule out confounding by formation of crosslinks
to other polypeptides. If a gel shift occurs only when both cysteine mutants in a pair are
present, it can be reasonably inferred that the crosslink is between those two species. It
is important to note that the chemistry of our crosslinking is different from that of
Natarajan et al., requiring mutations at two defined sites and allowing assessment of
crosslink specificity by the control permutations described.
Reviewer #2:
4) In the result section ‘The unliganded TCR-CD3 is closed and compacted in vivo’,
SDS-PAGE and Western blot analyses were done to identify crosslinks in the
unliganded closed conformation. A similar experiment in the presence of pMHC should
be done with the same mutant pairs (G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C and S78C-D77C). TCR
αβ-CD3δcrosslinks should be absent in the blots for these mutants as pMHC bound
form would lead to an ‘open’ conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. We feel this
experiment is crucial to support their overall result and conformation-change
hypothesis.
Authors’ response:
Unfortunately, the proposed experiment is not compatible with the engineered disulfide
system. The disulfides form on exposure to molecular oxygen during complex
assembly. Their formation is not temporally controlled.
We reiterate that the role of the engineered disulfide experiments was to test
whether the conformation of the unliganded TCR–CD3 in the cellular context is
empirically consistent with the observed conformation in nanodiscs or with that in
detergents. The ligand-bound conformation was then observed directly in nanodiscs
and is consistent with the ligand-bound form observed in detergents. We do not
hypothesize that the ligand-bound form in vivo would be distinct from that observed in
these two separate structural model systems. To reiterate, the point of this experiment
was to settle a conflict of physiological relevance between structural models from two
different systems, and no such conflict exists for the ligand-bound conformation.
Reviewer #2:
5) As indicated by the authors, in the ND-I and ND-II closed conformations, docking of
MHC-II-CD4 complex lead to hindrance with the lipid bilayers. This again brings into
question the physiological viability of the nanodiscs-bound complexes.
Authors’ response:
We disagree with the referee’s interpretation of these modeling results. We predict that
our ND-I and ND-II conformations are permissive for HLA binding by computational
modeling, and when we mix unliganded TCR in nanodiscs with HLA we indeed observe
complex formation (see ND-HLA structure). HLA binding to TCR–CD3 triggers a
conformational change into the open/extended conformation. We show by modeling that
the geometry of this conformation is permissive of TCR-pHLA-coreceptor ternary
complex formation. These results are entirely consistent with a model in which HLA
binds to the TCR, inducing a conformational change, which then permits ternary
complex formation and signal transduction.
Referee #2:
6) In the result section ‘HLA binding is sufficient to trigger TCR-CD3 conformational
change’, the authors use S104C-V182C mutant to lock the TCR in the ‘closed’
conformation which resulted in reduced signaling when compared to the WT upon
activation. The reason why the signal was not completely abolished is unclear. Perhaps
including multiple mutant pairs - G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C or S78C-D77C along with
S104C-V182C could completely lock the TCR in the closed conformation and thereby
totally abolish signaling.
Authors’ response:
While we agree that testing multiple pairs is indeed interesting and ongoing work will
address similar questions, this work is outside the scope of the current manuscript. We
show here a single engineered disulfide mutant pair with surface expression and ligand
binding comparable to wild type to avoid confounding from impaired surface expression
and/or receptor affinity. Identifying double or even triple engineered disulfides that do
not compromise these functions is likely to prove challenging. (As it stands, Reviewer
#5 finds even the single mutant’s surface expression to be unacceptable.)
There are several possible reasons for the partial amelioration of signaling. The
disulfide may not form reliably in 100% of cell surface-localized receptors, resulting in a
mixed population on the cell surface. Even if formed, the disulfide may not completely
prevent conformational change, perhaps allowing formation of intermediate
conformations, if not the open/extended conformation, per se. Lastly, ligand-induced
clustering may otherwise change the membrane milieu in ways that “tip the scales” to
allow for partial (suboptimal) signaling even without conformational change. None of
these hypothetical caveats are mutually exclusive. Nonetheless, the ability of this
mutant to reduce peak signaling with surface expression and ligand binding grossly
comparable to wild type is evidence of the importance of conformational change in the
process of ligand-induced receptor activation. We now discuss these caveats explicitly
in the text (lines 498-510).

Minor changes:
1) In line 53, ‘TCR-HLA interaction’ should be ‘TCR-pMHC interaction’.
Author’s response:
We have changed “TCR-HLA interaction” in line 51 to “TCR interaction with HLA–
antigen complex,” consistent with the human nomenclature used in this manuscript.
Reviewer #2:
2) The structure illustration in Figure 1b and the color scheme used is indecipherable.

Figure 1b shows an overlay of backbone representations for the published structures of

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
This study from Notti and colleagues provides structural insights into the inter-subunit
conformational relationships that can be assumed in the extracellular and
transmembrane domains within TCR-CD3 complexes when solubilized in detergent, or
when embedded within artificial membranes after reconstitution within nanodiscs. It
makes important additions to the growing library of available cryoEM structures of TCR-
CD3 complexes by providing examples embedded within membranes, which are
expected to be more physiological than detergent solubilized complexes. Unlike prior
detergent-soluble structures, showing the ectodomain of the TCR situated more upright
relative to the CD3 heterodimers, the two nanodisc-embedded structures (NDI and
NDII) adopt more closed arrangements with the TCR variable regions nearly touching
the tops of the CD3 heterodimers. In contrast, nanodisc-embedded TCR-CD3 bound to
pHLA adopt a more extended open structure in the ectodomain. The juxtamembrane
connecting peptides in the extracellular space, as well as the transmembrane domains
of the subunits, also show changes in the unliganded NDI/II conformations relative to
the liganded states. Notably, the transmembrane regions of the subunits adopt a
splayed relationship in the unliganded state that straightens in the liganded structures,
consistent with prior functional data. The authors conclude that the more compact NDI
and NDII complexes represent the resting state whereas the open configuration
represents a liganded signaling conformation, with changes in the orientation of the
constituent subunits in the ectodomain, extracellular juxtamembrane connecting
peptides, and transmembrane domains providing a mechanism by which pMHC
engagement leads to signaling across the membrane.
Experimentally, the study relies largely on cryoEM with some supporting biochemical
and functional data:
1. The investigators have the required expertise for the study. The structures appear to
be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that
could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures.
a. The lack of order in some regions creates some problems for insights into allosteric
changes for NDI and NDII.
Authors’ response:
We thank the reviewer for their careful and thoughtful analysis of the paper. As they
point out, we were conservative in our modeling of the structure, omitting regions where
disorder prevents reasonable modeling of protein backbone, sidechain, glycan, or lipid
atoms. Disorder-to-order transitions are functionally important and ubiquitous
throughout protein biochemistry. While such a transition precludes confident modeling
of disordered residues in static structures, that does not, in our view, detract from their
functional significance. Much in the way that allostery might be explained
mechanistically through a transition between two well-ordered states, it can also be
explained mechanistically through a disorder-to-order transition. Our data are in
agreement with the data reported by others showing rigidification of the TCR upon
ligand binding (references 15 and 32 in main text), suggesting this disorder-to-
order transition is mechanistically important for early TCR activation.
Reviewer #5:
2. The methods indicate that different combinations of constructs were used to purify
the TCR-CD3 complexes incorporated into nanodiscs for determination of unliganded
structures in NDI and ND2 than were used for the liganded complexes.
a. While unlikely, it is formally possible that changes in subunit tags, be they HIS or
EGFP or 2A tags left on the subunits, could differentially impact the spatial relationship
of the subunits within assembled complexes. What motivated the change in approach is
unclear but this caveat should be noted.
Authors’ response:
We agree that differences in carboxy-terminal tags are highly unlikely to explain
differences in conformation of the complex, given that the carboxy-termini of the TCR–
CD3 constituents are unstructured and thus not observed in the cryo-EM maps. When
we began this work, it was anticipated that tandem affinity purification would be needed
to obtain intact complex. This was fortunately not the case, and we thus simplified our
constructs during the course of this investigation. Nonetheless, the position of the His
tag is the same in all constructs used for cryo-EM, all constructs use furin cleavage site-
P2A linkers between complex components on the same virus, and all constructs have a
carboxy-terminal fluorescent protein fusion to TCRβ. In the three-virus expression
scheme, CD3ζ carries a carboxy-terminal EGFP fusion, which is separated from the
structured components by over 100 disordered amino acids; therefore, we think it
exceedingly unlikely that this would affect the structural models we report. Indeed, the
crosslinking studies were performed without a carboxy-terminal EGFP fusion on CD3ζ
and are consistent with the cryo-EM data. The rationale for vector simplification is now
noted in the text, lines 672-675.

paired used and the choice thereof.

conformation, but this did not yield any 3D reconstructions consistent with the
open/extended conformation. Analysis of 2D classification data (now in Supplementary
Fig. 2i,j) shows no classes of particles specifically suggestive of the open/extended
conformation. Despite due diligence to identify an open/extended subset of particles in
the resting state dataset, we do not detect this in our data.

b. The methods do not indicate the temperature at which the functional assays were

Reviewer #5:
e. The conclusions regarding Fig 7i and 7j are questionable given the data.
i. The histograms in Fig 7i clearly show lower expression of the S104C/V182C mutant
than the WT (note that the x-axis is on a log scale). The difference in tetramer staining,
as well as the difference in signaling in Fig 7j, could easily be due to differences in
surface expression of the WT and mutant TCRs.
ii. I recommend removing these data as they do not add to the study and could be
misinterpreted.
iii. For these data to be convincing, the investigators would need to make multiple
independently generated sets of Jurkat lines with matched TCR expression and show
that they consistently produced functional differences between the WT and Mut.
iv. The investigators should also show that the disulphide bonds are formed on TCR-
CD3 complexes that have translocated to the cell surface.
Authors’ response:
Relative to the untransfected control, surface expression of CD3ϵ, surface expression of
TCRβ, and ligand binding by the mutant are all grossly comparable to the wild type.
Indeed, this mutant-wild type pair compares quite favorably with other published
examples of engineered T-cell panels with purportedly “similar” ligand binding, including
from Nature Communications (e.g., Supplementary Fig. 3C in Finnigan et al., 2024;
PMID: 38459027). Nonetheless, we now show data for independently transduced TCR
clones, for which surface CD3ϵ, surface TCRβ, and HLA-tetramer binding in the TCRα
S104C/V182C mutant is at least numerically equivalent to (if not greater than) the wild
type (Supplementary Figure 8c, Supplementary Table 6). For these clones, we assayed
TCR activation in a more demanding and physiologically relevant system using HLA-
A*02:01-positive COS-7-A2 cells presenting NY-ESO-1 peptide to stimulate the reporter
cells instead of HLA-tetramers. In this more rigorous assay, we observed an even more
pronounced phenotype, with the mutant showing a 42% reduction in activated T cells
(Fig. 7i, Supplementary Table 7). We still include the data from the original clones
assayed with the HLA-tetramer assay, as they are from an independent clone set and
are consistent with these new data in a separate experimental system, but we have
moved them to the Supplement (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Table 5).
Regarding disulfide formation, we demonstrate robust disulfide formation for this
double-cysteine mutation pair by mass spectrometry (Figure 5e and Supplementary
Table 4). Although this analysis does not allow us to quantify the fraction of disulfide-
crosslinked TCRs on the cell surface in the Jurkat model, the mass spectrometry data
from HEK cells make it reasonable to infer that the disulfide is present in some fraction
of surface-expressed receptor complexes. We discuss in the main text the caveats
inherent in disulfide formation efficiency being unquantified.
Reviewer #5:
Title, Abstract, and Discussion level conclusions:
6. The structures provided herein are interesting and make an important contribution to
the field. They provide strong evidence that different inter-subunit conformational
relationships can be adopted by the transmembrane and connecting peptides of the
TCR-CD3 complex subunits. That alone is important information for the field.
7. The title and abstract level conclusions cannot fully be substantiated by the data and
should be calibrated to better reflect the limitations of the data.
a. The conclusion that the more closed NDI/II structures represent the resting state are
one of several plausible interpretations of the data. As the authors note, the T cell
membrane has variable subdomains with different lipid compositions, and it is unclear if
porcine neuron membranes are analogous to the membrane subdomain inhabited by
TCR-CD3 complexes on the T cell membrane.
b. Different environments will have different membrane curvatures (e.g., during
transport to the cell membrane or when localized at the tip of a filapodia). Given that the
complex is membrane-anchored during assembly and transport to the cell surface, the
different conformations may represent assembly or vesicular transport conformations
necessitated by the nature of those membrane.
Author’s response:
We agree that the membrane subdomains within a given cell are numerous, with
diverse physicochemical profiles. To say there is a single “native” membrane
environment, for example, would be overly simplistic. Future efforts are aimed at
determining how these various membrane environments alter TCR structure and
function. However, the data we show here are the first to determine the structure of the
TCR–CD3 complex in a lipid bilayer of any kind and is thus a priori a more plausible
model of the TCR–CD3 than any of the unliganded TCR–CD3 models from detergent,
which have been – and continue to be – published in the highest impact journals without
apparent concern for the physiological relevance of the micellar environment. Our
model is then supported empirically by the engineered disulfide crosslinking data from
human cells (this manuscript) as well as the independently generated photo-crosslinking
data from the Krogsgaard group (see discussion above; Natarajan et al., 2024, EMBO
Reports). Moreover, we show that the TCR–CD3 undergoes large conformational
changes in this model membrane environment in response to activating ligands,
providing further evidence that the ND-I/II conformational family represent a ligand-
receptive resting state. While this model may be nuanced by future studies of
membrane composition and geometry on TCR–CD3 structure and function, we argue
that our interpretation of the data has adequate empiric support and is the most
parsimonious explanation for the data at hand.
c. The effort to present functional data in Fig 7 to support their conclusions is not
convincing for the reasons outlined above. These data should be removed.
Authors’ response:
See above.
Reviewer #5:
8. The Discussion level conclusion “…that intrinsic conformational change in the TCR-
CD3 is necessary for early TCR-CD3 activation” is not fully substantiated by the data for
the reasons outlined above. However, discussing the structures presented here within
the context of biochemical and functional data from other studies that support their
interpretation would allow the authors to offer a plausible molecular mechanism for
those prior observations and lend confidence to the author’s contention that intrinsic
changes within the complex occur in the absence of intracellular kinase signaling.
a. In addition to the paper cited by the authors (PMID: 34260912), it would be relevant
to discuss studies showing exposure of cytoplasmic juxtamembrane proline rich
sequence on CD3e can occur in the absence of kinase signaling (even at 4ºC)(PMID:
12110186, 15728235).
b. Data that more directly complements the ligand-induced transmembrane allosteric
changes observed here, and which should also be noted for completeness, comes from
a study indicating that the zeta transmembrane domains are splayed in TCR-CD3 in the
resting state and move together in the liganded state in the absence of intracellular
signaling (PMID: 26231119).
Authors’ response:
Previous length limitations had unfortunately prevented us from including discussion of
a number of deserving studies from the vast, over four-decades-long TCR literature.
However, we have now been able to include the supplied references, and appreciate
the Reviewer’s assistance in curating these.
Reviewer #5:
9. The discussion regarding the potential role of glycosylation in regulating signaling is
interesting.
a. There is evidence for regulation of gdTCR-CD3 through differential glycosylation that
may be worth considering (PMID: 12438426).
Authors’ response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in the role of glycosylation in regulation of TCR
function. As the γδTCR has notable structural, functional, and biochemical differences
from the αβTCR – including the location of its glycosylation sites – we will
conservatively limit our discussion to the αβTCR for this manuscript.
Reviewer #5:
10. Evidence that TCR-CD3 inhabits specific membrane sub-domains that concatenate
with other distinct sub-domains (e.g., LAT containing domains) are worth consideration
(PMID: 20010844). If distinct membrane sub-domains have distinct thicknesses and
composition, this could force changes in intra- and inter-subunit transmembrane
orientations. They could also exchange sterols at the subdomain interface. They could
also potentially impact lipid-protein interactions at the conserved patches noted on CD3.
Authors’ response:
We agree with the reviewer’s inclination that lipid membrane environment may impact
TCR structure and function, and this work is ongoing, as discussed above.
Reviewer #5:
Regarding novelty, extensibility, broad interest and overall impact:
11. This study highlights the value of determining the structures of multi-subunit
complex in the membrane environment .
a. Doing so for the TCR-CD3 complex is highly novel.
12. This study provides key evidence that inter-subunit allosteric changes in the
transmembrane and juxtamembrane extracellular connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3
complex can occur upon ligand engagement.
a. This finding is not novel in the broad sense that evidence already exists for allosteric
changes in TCR-CD3 upon ligand engagement in the absence of other signaling events,
as noted above; nevertheless, it offers important molecular insights into how these
changes could occur.
b. A key strength of this study, for which it should make an important impact on the field,
is therefore derived from contributing to a growing body of evidence that such
conformational changes are the earliest events in TCR-CD3 signaling upon
engagement of cognate ligands.
13. This study is likely to be of broad interests to people who study multi-subunit
signaling receptors, lymphocyte activation, and receptor biology more broadly.
14. This study will also be of impact for its extensibility. The author’s present many key
findings that are idea generating, and these ideas are worth testing to work towards a
better understanding of this complex.

We thank the reviewer for their complementary assessment of our work’s novelty and
implications.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
REVIEWER COMMENTS AND AUTHORS’ RESPONSE
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
My concerns about severe preferred orientation issues in the 'closed and compacted'
conformation maps remain unaddressed. Based on our direct experience with
membrane protein complexes, such orientation bias can generate artifactual
'conformational differences' similar to those claimed here. Consequently, I find the
structural models and the corresponding interpretation unreliable.
That said, the functional data appear convincing (though I defer to TCR specialists for
final assessment). If other reviewers are satisfied, I support publication, as long as the
structural data caveats were mentioned in the paper. This study would be much more
impactful if supplemented with higher-quality cryo-EM data.
Authors’ response:
To address more fully the reviewer’s concerns about preferred orientation-induced
artifacts, we perform several computational analyses, which show that preferred particle
orientation cannot explain the observed closed, compacted conformation seen in 3D
reconstructions from the ND dataset. Specifically, we test whether the paucity of
straight-on “side views” (views parallel to the membrane plane) in the ND
reconstructions relative to the GDN dataset (Supplementary Figure 2i) could artifactually
yield a 3D reconstruction in the closed, compacted conformation. To do this, we 2D
classified the 251k particles in the final GDN reconstruction into 50 classes and
removed classes corresponding to true side views, as well as remaining poorly aligned
particles (Response Figure 1a). Tilted views in between a “side” and “top” (membrane
normal) view were retained, as analogous views are seen in the ND dataset
(Supplementary Figure 2i). Using the selected 155k particles, we performed ab initio
reconstruction, nonuniform refinement, and local refinement as in the main manuscript.
3D reconstruction from this particle stack showed a similar preferred particle orientation
to the ND reconstructions, as shown by a similar 3D FSC profile (Response Figure 1b,
left), but still generated an unambiguously open, extended 3D reconstruction (Response
Figure 1b, right). This shows that a preferred particle orientation resulting in a relative
deficiency of side views of the TCR–CD3 complex is not sufficient to generate an
artifactually closed, compacted reconstruction. Moreover, if we seed reconstruction of
this 155k particle set with the ND-II conformation as a starting model (instead of an
unbiased ab initio model), the refinement fails to yield a high-resolution reconstruction
and the 3D FSC curve declines linearly with a different morphology than that seen in the
ND dataset (Response Figure 1c). Taken together, these results show that deficiency of
side views from a dataset with an open, extended “ground truth” conformation is not
sufficient to cause artifactual closure and compaction, even when attempting to bias the
data processing towards this result.
Response Figure 1: Computational analysis of the impact of preferred orientation
on closure and compaction of TCR–CD3 3D reconstruction
To highlight our experimental efforts to improve map quality, we here show density for
the TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs reconstruction from 425k particles on graphene
oxide coated-grids with fluorinated Fos-choline present. 3D reconstructions still show a
closed, compacted complex, but the preferred particle orientation persists, and the
reconstructions are not of noticeably higher quality (Response Figure 2).
Response Figure 2: Example reconstruction of the TCR–CD3 complex in
nanodiscs from graphene oxide grids with fluorinated Fos-choline present.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
After review of the revised manuscript, I feel that the authors have addressed all
concerns satisfactorily and I recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature
Communications. The work presented is extensive and addressed an important problem
involving TCR activation.
Many findings of Natarajan et al., EMBO Reports, 2024 was corroborated by the
present work. We thank the authors for the detailed discussion (with figures in the
supplementary section) of the work by Natarajan et al. especially - 1) explaining the
compatibility of different crosslinks obtained between Cβ CC’ loop-CD3δ, Cβ FG loop –
CD3γ, Cβ helix 4 – F strand- CD3δ/CD3ε and the ND-based open cryo-EM structure; 2)
detailing the reason for lack of changes in crosslinks between CD3δ D77-TCRα in the
presence and absence of pMHC tetramers.
Authors’ response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the synergy of these two datasets.
While critiquing the findings of Natarajan et al., the authors incorrectly state that the
binding ability of FG loop targeting H57 antibody to W225-pAzpa mutant complex wasn’t
assessed in the study. Although lower than other mutant complexes W225-pAzpa
showed reasonable H57 antibody binding (Appendix Figure S4 in Natarajan et al.).This

Authors’ response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this figure panel in the Supplementary Data of
Natarajan et al. (2024) EMBO J. We have removed discussion of the FG-loop mutants
from the manuscript.
In Fig 7h and 7i, my previous concern regarding testing only one mutant – S104C-
V182C is not addressed satisfactorily. It is completely unclear why testing multiple
mutants were outside the scope of the present study. This must be clarified. If not for
testing multiple mutant pairs involving G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C and S78C-D77C
combinedly, at least one of these alternate pairs could have been tested to strengthen
their hypothesis. I understand the concern regarding complex expression which was
raised by another reviewer. But the cells can be sorted for comparable expression of the

Authors’ response:
We now include additional data for an opening-constraining TCRβ disulfide mutant
(T130C/H172C). We previously demonstrated disulfide formation for this mutant by
mass spectrometry (Figure 5 d,f). Here we show that despite greater-than-wildtype
surface expression (Supplementary Figure 8e,f and source data in Supplementary
Table 8), this mutant shows a significantly attenuated response to peptide-HLA
stimulation (Supplementary Figure 8g and source data in Supplementary Table 9). This
phenotype is consistent with the results we have already shown for the TCRα disulfide
mutant (S140C/V182C) and provide further support for the hypothesis that
conformational change is critical for ligand-dependent TCR activation. We also show
data for our efforts to test other conformation-constraining mutants. We include flow
cytometry characterization for two disulfide mutants predicted to prevent TCR–CD3
extension (TCRβ Q220C/V274C and TCRβ R223C/L275C; Supplementary Figure 8e,f
and source data in Supplementary Table 8). Both mutants show a significant reduction
