## Methods

Plasmids and sequences
A modified version of the BacMam expression system47 was used for the expression of the TCR–CD3 complex in HEK cells with furin cleavage and P2A ribosomal skipping sites separating each protein sequence (see below, Protein expression and purification and Engineered disulfide crosslinking). The modified viral vector also expressed the VSV-g sequence (kind gift from Titia de Lange, Rockefeller University) under a baculoviral promoter to enhance mammalian cell tropism. A self-inactivating retroviral plasmid encoding the 1G4(LY) TCRαβ sequence (wild type for this study) was a kind gift from S.A. Rosenberg, NIH. CD3ζ was cloned from Jurkat cell cDNA using standard restriction enzyme-based approaches. Similarly, CD3ϵ, CD3γ, CD3δ, EGFP, mCherry, and 8xHis tags were cloned from synthetic double-stranded DNA blocks (IDT DNA). Mutant TCR–CD3 sequences were produced by overlap-extension PCR or synthesized de novo (Genscript). Construct sequences can be found in and following Supplementary Table 10.

E. coli strains
Bacteria were grown under standard conditions: 37°C, ambient CO2; LB broth shaking 200 rpm for liquid cultures, LB agar for plates. DH5α (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 18265017) were used for cloning and amplification of plasmid DNA, and BL21(DE3) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, EC0114) were used for MSP expression. DH10Bac cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10361012) were grown as per manufacturer instructions for the recombination of plasmid DNA into bacmids.

Eukaryotic cell lines
Insect and human cells lines were maintained under standard sterile conditions using aseptic technique with the following parameters: SF-9 cells (ATCC, CRL-1711) were maintained at 5×105-1×106 cells/mL in Sf-900 II SFM medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with antibiotic-antimycotic solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 27°C, ambient CO2. HEK293GP cells (Takara Bio, 631458) and derivatives were maintained at 10-90% confluency in RPMI medium 1640 (RPMI, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Sigma Aldrich), 10 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, and penicillin/streptomycin at 37°C, 5% CO2. HEK293F FreeStyle cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R79007) were maintained at 5×105 to 2×106 cells/mL in FreeStyle 293 expression medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with antibiotic-antimycotic solution at 37°C, 8% CO2. Modified Jurkat T cells (see below, Generation of an NFAT-reporter cell line) and COS-7-A2 cells were maintained at 2×105 to 2×106 cells/mL in RPMI medium supplemented with 10% FBS and penicillin-streptomycin solution at 37°C, 5% CO2. HEK cells are of female human origin and Jurkat cells are of male human origin. COS-7-A2 cells was gifted by Dr. Steven Rosenberg (NIH) and derived from the male African green monkey cell line COS-7 with stable transduction of human HLA-A*02:01. Cell line identify was validated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).

Baculovirus production
Bacmid recombineering was performed as per manufacturer specifications with the FastBac system in DH10Bac cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Bacmid was purified by phenol/chloroform/isoamyl alcohol extraction, and approximately 25 μg bacmid DNA was transfected into SF-9 cells adherent in 6-well plates using Cellfectin II reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in Grace’s Insect Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 6 h at 27°C before transfer to Sf-900 II SFM medium supplemented with antibiotic-antimycotic solution. After 5 days, the cell supernatant (P1 virus) was removed and used to inoculate a 40-mL culture of SF-9 cells at 1×106 cells/mL. After >50% of the cells had died (~day 5), supernatant (P2 virus) was harvested by centrifugation of the culture at 3500×g for 20 min, decanted, supplemented with 2% FBS, and stored in the dark at 4°C. For large-scale expression, P3 virus was produced by inoculating 40-mL cultures of SF-9 cells at 3×106 cells/mL with 2 mL P2 virus and cultured, harvested, and stored as for P2 virus.

Protein expression, purification, and nanodisc reconstitution
See overview schematic in Fig. 1a. For structural studies, ~250-mL cultures of HEK293F FreeStyle cells at 2×106 cells/mL shaking in 1-L baffled polycarbonate flasks were inoculated with 15 mL each of P3 virus, and sodium butyrate (Alfa Aesar) was added to a final concentration of 10 mM to enhance expression. For preparation of the TCR–CD3 in detergent for cryo-EM, TCR–CD3 was expressed using two baculoviruses: (1) TCRα-[furin/P2A]-TCRβ::mCherry, and (2) CD3ϵ-[furin/P2A]-CD3ζ-[furin/P2A]-CD3δ-[furin/P2A]-CD3γ::8HIS. Cells were incubated at 30°C, 5% CO2 for 3 days to allow expression and harvested by centrifugation at 4000×g for 10 min at 4°C. Cell pellets were resuspended in 25 mM HEPES (Sigma Aldrich), pH 7.5, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (Sigma Aldrich) and lysed with a Dounce homogenizer. Lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 4000×g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was decanted and ultracentrifuged at 100,000×g for 1 h at 4°C to recover the membrane fraction. Membrane pellets were resuspended in 25 mM HEPES (Sigma Aldrich), pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl (Thermo Fisher Scientific), herein HBS, and n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM, Anatrace) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS, Anatrace) were added to final concentrations of 1% and 0.2%, respectively. The membrane pellets were solubilized on a rotator for 2 h at 4°C. Debris was removed by centrifugation at 4000×g for 30 min at 4°C. The clarified supernatant was loaded onto NiNTA-agarose resin (Qiagen). Resin was washed with 50 column volumes of HBS with 0.02% glyco-diosgenin (GDN) and 30 mM imidazole (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The TCR–CD3 was eluted from the NiNTA-agarose resin with 360 mM imidazole and 0.02% GDN in HBS. The mCherry fusion to TCRβ was removed by incubation with human rhinovirus protease 3C overnight at 4°C. Protein was concentrated with Amicon centrifugal filters (Millipore) and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography in HBS with 0.02% GDN over a Superose 6 column (GE Healthcare).

For expression of the TCR–CD3 for affinity purification and nanodisc reconstitution, we found that co-expression of three viral constructs gave acceptable yields of material for cryo-EM analysis: (1) TCRα-[furin/P2A]-TCRβ::mCherry-[furin/P2A]-CD3δ-[furin/P2A]-CD3γ-[furin/P2A]-CD3ϵ-[furin/P2A]-CD3ζ::EGFP, (2) CD3δ-[furin/P2A]-CD3γ::8HIS, and (3) CD3ϵ-[furin/P2A]-CD3ζ::EGFP. This three-virus expression scheme was later simplified to two viruses for studies with HLA-bound (below), in detergent (above), or TCR–CD3 crosslinking experiments, as tandem affinity purification was not found to be necessary for intact complex recovery. Cells were cultured, infected, harvested, and lysed as above. Lysate was clarified, membranes isolated and extracted, and extracts loaded onto NiNTA-agarose resin as above. Resin was washed with 50 column volumes of HBS with 0.1% DDM, 0.02% CHS, and 30 mM imidazole. The resin was resuspended in HBS with 0.1% DDM, 0.02% CHS for on-bead nanodisc reconstitution. For the TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs subsequently incubated with HLA–β2M–NY-ESO-1, a simplified two-virus expression scheme was used: (1) TCRα-[furin/P2A]-TCRβ::EGFP, and (2) CD3ϵ-[furin/P2A]-CD3ζ-[furin/P2A]-CD3δ-[furin/P2A]-CD3γ::8HIS. Protein complexes were otherwise purified as above.

T-cell subsets differ in plasma membrane lipid composition, and individual T cells have spatially heterogenous membrane compositions17. To create a lipid environment with a diversity of lipid constituents, including the negatively charged phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylinositol lipids important for ITAM–membrane interactions9,10, porcine brain polar lipids (Avanti Polar Lipids #141101C) were used to reconstitute the lipid bilayer. Avanti reports the composition of this lipid mixture as follows: 12.6% phosphatidylcholines, 33.1% phosphatidylethanolamines, 4.1% phosphatidylinositides, 18.5% phosphatidylserines, 0.8% phosphatidic acid, 30.9% unknown. The porcine brain polar lipids dissolved in 10% DDM were added to a final concentration of 33 mg/mL (approximately 43 μM using the molecular weight of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-glycero-3-phosphocholine as a standard phospholipid) and membrane-scaffold protein (MSP) 1D1ΔH5 was added to a final concentration of 20 μM. MSP 1D1ΔH5 was expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3), NiNTA-affinity purified, and affinity tags removed with TEV protease as previously described48 after subcloning from pET28a-MSP1D1ΔH5 (a gift from Gerhard Wagner, Addgene plasmid # 71714)49. Nanodisc reconstitution components were allowed to incubate for 15 min on ice before addition of SM-2 BioBeads (Bio-Rad) to approximately ¼ of the reaction volume. The mixture was incubated overnight on a rotator at 4°C. The reaction mixture was again returned to a disposable plastic column and washed with 20 column volumes of HBS, 50 column volumes of HBS with NaCl increased to 300 mM and 30 mM imidazole, washed with 20 column volumes of HBS, then eluted in HBS with 360 mM imidazole. Protein was concentrated with Amicon centrifugal filters (Millipore) and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography in HBS over a Superose 6 column (GE Healthcare). Peak fractions were collected and their quality ensured by SDS-PAGE followed by silver staining (Invitrogen), Coomassie blue staining, or Acquastain (Bulldog Bio) as per manufacturer specifications, and by negative-stain electron microscopy as described previously50. Briefly, samples were adsorbed for 30 s to glow-discharged, carbon-coated copper grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences), washed three times in deionized water, stained in freshly prepared 0.7% uranyl formate, and air dried before imaging on a CM-10 transmission electron microscope (Philips) equipped with XR-16 detector (Advanced Microscopy Techniques).

Cryo-EM specimen preparation and data collection
For the TCR–CD3 in GDN, Superose 6 peak fractions were concentrated with Amicon centrifugal concentrators to 5 mg/mL as determined with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) assuming 1 AU = 1 mg/mL. Aliquots of 4 μL were applied to glow-discharged 400 mesh R1.2/1.3 Cu grids with graphene oxide (Quantifoil) using a Vitrobot Mark VI (Thermo Fisher Scientific) set at 4°C and 100% humidity. After 20 s, grids were blotted for 0.5 s with a blot force of −2 and plunged into liquid nitrogen-cooled ethane.

For the TCR–CD3 in nanodisc sample, Superose 6 peak fractions were concentrated with Amicon centrifugal concentrators to 330 μg/mL as determined with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer assuming 1 AU = 1 mg/mL. Aliquots of 4 μL were applied to glow-discharged 400 mesh R1.2/1.3 Cu grids using a Vitrobot Mark VI set at 4°C and 100% humidity. After 5 s, grids were blotted for 4 s with a blot force of −2 and plunged into liquid nitrogen-cooled ethane. For the TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs with HLA–β2M–NY-ESO-1, the Superose 6 peak fractions were concentrated with Amicon centrifugal concentrators to 600 μg/mL. Lyophilized HLA single-chain trimer (herein, “HLA”; fusion of NY-ESO-1 C9V [SLLMWITQV], β2M I21-M119, and HLA-A*02:01 G25-T305; Kactus Biologics) was dissolved in deionized water per manufacturer instructions and then re-purified by size-exclusion chromatography over a Superose 6 column into HBS to remove PBS and trehalose and concentrated to 1 mg/mL. The TCR–CD3 and HLA single-chain trimer were mixed at a 2:1 volume ratio (1:5 approximate molar ratio). Aliquots of 4 μL were applied to glow-discharged graphene oxide-coated 400 mesh R1.2/1.3 Cu grids (Quantifoil) using a Vitrobot Mark VI (Thermo Fisher Scientific) set at 4°C and 100% humidity. After a wait time of 20 s, grids were blotted for 0.5 s with a blot force of −2 and plunged into liquid nitrogen-cooled ethane.

Cryo-EM imaging was performed in the Cryo-EM Resource Center at The Rockefeller University using SerialEM v4.1.0 beta51. Data collection parameters are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. In brief, for all samples, data were collected on a 300-kV Titan Krios electron microscope at a nominal magnification of 64,000×, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 1.08 Å on the specimen level. Images were collected with a K3 direct electron detector (Gatan) in super-resolution counting mode. The superfast mode in SerialEM was used, in which 3×3 holes are exposed using beam tilt and image shift before moving the stage to the next position52.

For the TCR–CD3 in detergent sample, images were collected using a defocus range of −0.8 to −2.5 μm. Exposures of 2.0 s were dose-fractionated into 50 frames (40 ms per frame) with a dose rate of 30 electrons per pixel per s (approximately 1.03 electrons per Å2 per frame), resulting in a total dose of 51 electrons per Å2. For the TCR–CD3 in nanodisc sample, images were collected using a defocus range of −0.8 to −2.0 μm. Exposures of 2.2 s were dose-fractionated into 55 frames (40 ms per frame) with a dose rate of 30 electrons per pixel per s (approximately 1.03 electrons per Å2 per frame), resulting in a total dose of 57 electrons per Å2. For the HLA-bound TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs sample, images were collected using a defocus range of −0.8 to −2.0 μm. Exposures of 2.0 s were dose-fractionated into 50 frames (40 ms per frame) with a dose rate of 30 electrons per pixel per s (approximately 1.03 electrons per Å2 per frame), resulting in a total dose of 51 electrons per Å2.

Cryo-EM image processing for the TCR–CD3 in detergent
The 15,726 collected movie stacks were gain-normalized, motion-corrected, dose-weighted, and binned over 2 × 2 pixels in MotionCor2 v1.1.053 and imported into cryoSPARC v4.2 for all further processing (see data processing overview and motion-corrected micrograph examples in Supplementary Fig. 1). A subset of the larger dataset, comprising 4,278 micrographs, was used to generate an initial model. The contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were determined with CTFFIND v455 implemented in cryoSPARC. Micrographs were curated by average defocus value, CTF fit resolution and CTF cross correlation, yielding 3,292 motion-corrected micrographs with CTF estimations for downstream processing. Particles were picked with the cryoSPARC blob-picker using a size range of 80 to 180 Å. These initial particles were filtered by power level and normalized cross-correlation score. Particles were subjected to serial rounds of 2D classification, wherein particles with the best alignment, as determined quantitatively by resolution estimate or qualitatively by appearance of fine structure, were advanced to the next round of 2D classification and selection. The best 82k particles were used for ab initio modeling, specifying three models. One model was clearly recognizable as TCR–CD3 in a detergent micelle; the other two models were amorphous blobs. All three models were used to seed 3D heterogeneous refinement using the same 82k particles, and the resulting TCR–CD3 model was used as an initial model in downstream processing.

We returned to the full dataset of 15,726 motion-corrected micrographs. CTF parameters were estimated using Patch CTF in cryoSPARC. Micrographs were curated by average defocus value, defocus range, CTF fit resolution, and relative ice thickness, yielding 15,153 micrographs for particle picking. Particles were picked with 20-Å lowpass-filtered templates from the model of the TCR–CD3 in detergent determined above and filtered by power level and normalized cross-correlation score. Particles were subjected to serial 2D classification as above and 3D classification by multireference refinement (using the heterogeneous refinement job in cryoSPARC). Serial rounds of 3D classification were seeded with the best available model along with decoy noise models to remove poorly aligning particles. Decoy classes were created by aborting ab initio modeling jobs after the first round of modeling before any structure was visible. The best aligning particles emerging from 3D classification were then used to train a Topaz (v 0.2.5a) particle picking model56 in cryoSPARC and the resulting particle stacks subjected to iterative rounds of 2D classification, 3D variability analysis, 3D classification, Topaz retraining, and particle pooling until map quality reached a plateau.

Picking from the 15,153-micrograph set with the best Topaz model yielded 2M particles. These particles were subjected to serial 2D classification, and the best 951k particles were entered into three rounds of serial 3D classification seeded with the best prior model and three noise decoys. This yielded 311k particles which were subjected to an additional round of 2D classification, from which 248k particles were selected. These particles, along with those from the best prior Topaz-picked model (242k), were re-extracted in 300×300-pixel boxes and pooled to ensure that all high-quality particles were captured for final reconstruction. One round of 2D classification was performed on the extracted particles and duplicates removed, yielding 388k unique particles. Of these, the 310k best-aligning particles were selected to advance into a final cascade of five rounds of serial 3D classification seeded with the best prior model and 3 noise decoys. The final 252k particle set emerging from these classifications was subjected to non-uniform refinement, yielding a map with nominal resolution of 3.3 Å. For this and all nominal resolutions listed herein, resolutions are reported from gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) curves with a cut-off criterion of 0.143. Local refinement with a mask including the protein components but excluding the micelle density further improved map quality and interpretability.

Cryo-EM image processing for the TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs
The 17,766 collected movie stacks were gain-normalized, motion-corrected, dose-weighted, binned over 2 × 2 pixels, and CTF parameters estimated as above for GDN (see data processing streams and motion-corrected micrograph examples in Supplementary Fig. 2). Micrographs were curated by CTF fit resolution and cross correlation, yielding 14,852 motion-corrected micrographs with CTF estimations for downstream processing.

Three parallel processing streams were pursued based on different approaches to particle picking (Supplementary Fig. 2). Particles were picked in cryoSPARC using (1) an unbiased blob-picking approach using a particle size range of 60 to 120 Å, (2) a template-based approach with a model of the TCR–CD3 in detergent (PBD 6JXR5) docked into the MSP1D1DH5 nanodisc using the CHARMM-GUI web server [https://www.charmm-gui.org/]57 nanodisc builder58, and (3) a template-based approach using the structure of the TCR–CD3 in detergent (PBD 6JXR5). For each processing stream, 2D image classification was performed on 4×4 binned particle images to eliminate classes of noise or poorly aligning particles and ab initio modeling was performed. At this stage, it was clear that the particles picked using 6JXR templates were of poor quality and did not yield reconstructions substantially different from those obtained with the other two processing streams (see below) and this avenue was thus aborted. For the other two streams, particle stacks were subjected to iterative rounds of 2D classification, ab initio modeling, 3D variability analysis, and 3D classification until map quality plateaued. The best aligning particles from these two streams were pooled and iterative rounds of 2D classification, 3D classification, Topaz training, and particle pooling was performed until map quality plateaued.

Having now exhaustively sampled the micrographs for well-aligning particles, the best aligning 2.2M unique particles were extracted into 256×256-pixel boxes without binning. After one round of 2D classification and selection, 1.8M particles remained. These particles were subjected to two rounds of serial 3D heterogenous refinement seeded with the best two available maps along with two noise maps, yielding 630k and 809k particles in the two best classes. After re-extraction into 300×300-pixel boxes without binning, these two classes, which we now denote ND-I and ND-II, contained 620k and 797k particles and refined to nominal resolutions of 3.2 Å and 3.0 Å, respectively. Local refinement with a mask including the protein components but excluding the nanodisc density further improved map quality and interpretability.

Cryo-EM image processing for the TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs incubated with HLA
The 13,644 collected movie stacks gain-normalized, motion-corrected, dose-weighted, binned over 2 × 2 pixels, and CTF parameters estimated as above for GDN, ND-I, and ND-II (see data processing stream and motion-corrected micrograph examples in Supplementary Fig. 7). Micrographs were curated by average defocus, astigmatism, CTF fit resolution, and CTF fit cross correlation, yielding 10,610 motion-corrected micrographs with CTF estimations for downstream processing. Particles were initially picked by a template-based approach using a model of the TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs ND-II conformation with HLA from PDB 2BNQ59 docked by alignment of the TCR variable domains. Templates were 20-Å lowpass-filtered prior to particle picking. These initial particles were filtered by power level and normalized cross-correlation score and subjected to iterative 2D classification, ab initio modeling, 3D classification (by heterogeneous refinement and by 3D classification without alignment), and Topaz training.

To ensure exhaustive sampling of the available data, particle picks from the best three Topaz models were pooled and duplicate particles removed, yielding 3.3M unique particles. These particles were extracted in 400×400-pixel boxes (binned 2×2) to ensure adequate accommodation for delocalized signal around the elongated TCR–CD3–HLA particles. One round of 3D heterogenous refinement was performed, seeded with the best two maps (one showing strong HLA density and one showing weaker HLA density) from the prior 3D classifications alongside 2 decoy maps. The 895k particles aligning to the HLA-strong model were subjected to an additional cycle of 3D classification without alignment, seeded by principal component analysis and specifying six classes. The six output volumes were used as the starting classes for one round of heterogeneous refinement with the 895k-particle set. One class comprising 192k particles refined to higher resolution than the others. The same analysis (3D classification without alignment followed by 3D heterogenous refinement) was performed for the HLA-weak set, yielding a single high-resolution class with 215k particles. These two sets of particles were re-extracted into a 400×400-pixel box without binning, and combined with the prior best particle stack, comprising 297k particles, also extracted now in a 400×400-pixel box. Duplicate particles were removed, yielding 587k unique particles. These particles were subjected to four rounds of serial 3D heterogeneous refinement seeded with the HLA-strong and HLA-weak models, with the particles classifying in the HLA-strong class advancing to the next round. This yielded 155k particles in the final set. Non-uniform refinement of this particle set yielded a map with a nominal resolution of 3.6 Å. Local refinement was performed with a custom mask excluding the bulk lipid of the nanodisc, yielding a map with a nominal resolution of 3.5 Å. This map was used for refinement in Phenix. Additional local refinements on subsets of the structure (e.g., TCR variable domains – HLA) were performed and used to guide manual model building but were not used for final refinement or calculation of refinement statistics.

Cryo-EM map assessment and post-processing
Gold-standard FSC curves were generated in cryoSPARC during refinement and nominal resolutions are reported with a cut-off criterion of 0.143. FSC curves for final maps are shown in Supplementary Figs. 1, 2, 7. Map anisotropy was assessed with 3DFSC60 implemented in cryoSPARC, and local resolution analysis was also performed in cryoSPARC (Supplementary Figs. 1, 2, 7). Although all models were refined against unsharpened maps (see Model building and refinement, below), sharpened maps were used for visual interpretation, manual model building, and figure generation. Map sharpening (Supplementary Fig. 3) was performed either by global B-factor approaches (better visualization of lipid densities) or DeepEMhancer v0.1461 (better visualization of protein densities).

Model building and refinement
The model of TCR–CD3 in GDN micelles was built starting with rigid-body docking of prior models in ChimeraX v1.6.1-1.1062. Specifically, PDB 6JXR was used as a starting model for the CD3 proteins and the TCR constant regions and transmembrane helices, PDB 7FJD was used to dock the cholesterols, and PDB 6BNU59 was used as a starting model for the 1G4 TCR variable regions. This starting model readily docked into the map, anchored by the clear alignment of immunoglobulin folds to the map features and continuous density for all chains through the ectodomains, juxtamembrane linkers, and transmembrane helices (see example densities in Supplementary Fig. 3). As with prior TCR–CD3 structures, the cytoplasmic unstructured regions were not resolved in the map. The model was improved by iterative cycles of refinement with phenix.real_space_refine in PHENIX v1.20.163, manual adjustment in Coot v0.9.8.764, and brief map-constrained relaxation in ISOLDE v1.965. Residues without clear side-chain density beyond Cβ were manually modeled as stubs. Cores for the N-linked glycans were built in Coot using tools included in the package66 (modeled glycans indicated graphically in Supplementary Fig. 6d). For all models, refinement data are shown in Supplementary Table 2, and model completeness is shown in Supplementary Table 3. All cryo-EM map and molecular model figures were generated in ChimeraX.

For the ND-I and ND-II models, the TCR–CD3-in-GDN model built above was used as a starting model and domains were docked into the map in ChimeraX. Again, the immunoglobulin folds in the TCR and CD3 ectodomains were readily anchored into the map features, with bulky hydrophobic residues and disulfide bonds periodically confirming register (map density overviews and sections shown in Supplementary Fig. 3). Regions without clear density in the maps were removed and residues without clear side-chain density beyond Cβ were manually modeled as stubs. For the CD3ϵ, CD3γ, and CD3δ proteins, the register for the juxtamembrane linker and transmembrane helices were anchored by the placement of the C-X-X-C liats at the beginning of the juxtamembrane region (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Bulky hydrophobic side chains provided further confirmation of register within the transmembrane helices. In ND-I, the register at the amino-terminus of the CD3ϵG transmembrane helix could not be unambiguously determined, so this helix was left unmodeled. For CD3ζ, the GDN model of these chains was docked in place and manually refit, using the interchain disulfide bond and bulky hydrophobic residues to confirm register (Supplementary Fig. 3g). For TCRα and TCRβ, the linker peptides between their constant domains and the transmembrane helices were poorly structured and left unmodeled. Their transmembrane helices were docked from the GDN structure relative to the surrounding helices and bulky side chains were used to confirm register (Supplementary Fig. 3h). Model building and refinement was performed in Phenix, Coot, ChimeraX, and ISOLDE as described above for the TCR–CD3-in-GDN structure.

For the TCR–CD3–HLA structure, the GDN structure readily docked into the cryo-EM map. The HLA–β2M–NY-ESO-1 structure from PDB 2BNQ59 was docked into the map. The structure was refined in Phenix as described above. Example density with constructed model is shown in Supplementary Fig. 7j.

Sequence conservation analysis
TCR and CD79-BCR sequences were analyzed using the Consurf67 web server [https://consurf.tau.ac.il/] and colored according to relative sequence conservation level in ChimeraX. For computation of sequence identity among GDN and the published TCR–CD3 structures in detergent, sequences were aligned with the Clustal Omega web server [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/msa/clustalo]68.

Engineered disulfide-bond analysis
Cysteine mutant pairs were designed with the Cα-Cα parameters described in the main text. For Western blot analysis, HEK293F cells were plated at 1.5×106 cells/mL in 6-well plates, 2 mL per well. Cells were infected with baculovirus expressing the indicated TCR–CD3 mutants at a volume 1/30 the culture volume and the indicated CD3 mutants at 1/15 the culture volume. All TCRα mutants were paired with the same wild-type TCRβ sequence. 10 mM sodium butyrate was added at the same time as viral infection to enhance expression. Cultures were incubated for 2 days at 37°C, 8% CO2. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 20,800×g, and resuspended in Laemmli sample buffer with or without 100 mM dithiothreitol (GoldBio). Samples were heated for 5 min at 95°C prior to separation by SDS-PAGE. Gels were electroblotted to immobilon-P PVDF membranes (Millipore), rinsed in 200 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris (Research Products International), pH 8 (TBS), supplemented with 0.05% Tween-20 (TBST, Sigma Aldrich), and blocked in neat Intercept Blocking Buffer (Li-Cor) for 1 h at room temperature. Blots were incubated with mouse anti-GFP antibody (1:3,000, Roche/Sigma Aldrich, Cat. # 11814460001) in TBST with 10% block overnight at 4°C. Blots were washed with TBST at 25°C, incubated with Alexa 700-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1:10,000, Invitrogen, Cat. # A-21036) in TBST with 10% block at 25°C for 1 h, and again washed sequentially with TBST and TBS. Blots were imaged on an Amersham Typhoon infrared fluorescence scanner.

To confirm the results seen in whole-cell lysates, mutant TCR–CD3 was also detergent extracted from membrane pellets and NiNTA-affinity purified, as was done for cryo-EM analyses, and NiNTA elutions in DDM/CHS were processed for Western blot analysis. To further confirm that these crosslinks were formed in properly assembled TCR–CD3 complexes, select disulfide-bond mutants were also reconstituted into nanodiscs and purified by size-exclusion chromatography, by the same protocol used for producing TCR–CD3 in nanodiscs for cryo-EM analysis. For these samples, protein constituents were visualized in gels using Acquastain as per manufacturer specifications.

Mass spectrometry
Protein was produced as for structural studies but using the indicated mutant TCR–CD3 constructs with TCRβ fused to EGFP and CD3ζ untagged. The CD3 proteins, including 8xHis-tagged CD3γ were expressed from a single virus. Instead of reconstitution into nanodiscs, the TCR–CD3 complex was eluted from NiNTA-agarose resin in HBS containing DDM/CHS, free cysteines were blocked with 20 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma Aldrich) in the dark for 1 h at room temperature. The reaction was quenched, and detergent was removed by acetone precipitation. Protein complexes were deglycosylated with PNGase F and sequentially digested using sequencing-grade trypsin for 3 h, followed by a second digestion step using chymotrypsin for another 3 h. Enzymatic activity was quenched by acidification using trifluoroacetic acid and the resulting peptides were purified using in-house constructed C18 micropurification tips prior to LC-MS MS analysis69. Peptides were separated across a 70-min linear gradient, in which the fraction of solvent B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) over solvent A (1% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) was increased from 2% to 35% using an Easy nLC 1200 Ultra-High Performance Liquid Chromatography system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a 100 μm-by-120 μm pulled-emitter column packed with 3-μm C18 material (Nikkyo Technos). Analysis was carried out using a Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating in positive-ion DDA, FT-mode. Ions were fragmented using EThcD. Disulfide bonds were identified using the XlinkX software through Proteome Discoverer v. 2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Generation of an NFAT-reporter cell line
The J8Zb2m-α-β- cell line for TCR–CD3 display was generated as follows: The Jurkat-derived cell line J.RT3-T3.5 (ATCC, TIB-153) lacking endogenous TCRβ chain was modified to express an NFAT reporter and CD8 via transduction with retroviral supernatant from HEK293GP-GLV9 producer cells transfected with the 8xNFAT-ZsG-hCD8 plasmid (a gift from Maki Nakayama, Addgene plasmid # 153417)70,71. 48 h post transduction, transductants were stimulated with PMA/Ionomycin overnight and sorted on CD8+ZsGreen+ cells using a Sony SH800. Sorted cells were allowed to recover in vitro for 5 days and subsequently nucleofected using a Nucleofector IIb device (Program X-001) with β2M sgRNA (5’-CGCGAGCACAGCUAAGGCCA-3’; Synthego) pre-complexed with TrueCut Cas9 V2 (Invitrogen, A26498) according to the manufacturer’s recommendation. Nucleofected cells were allowed to recover in RPMI + 2 mM L-glutamine + 20% FCS without antibiotics for 2 days and thereafter HLA-ABC- live cells were sorted using a Sony SH800.

To then render the resulting cell line deficient for the TCRα chain, TRAC gene sgRNA (5’-TCTCTCAGCTGGTACACGGC-3’; IDT) and Alt-R S.p. Cas9 Nuclease V3 (IDT 1081058) were introduced using a Lonza 4D-Nucleofector. TRAC knock-out was confirmed by ICE CRISPR Analysis Tool v3 (Synthego) using Sanger sequencing data flanking the edited cut site. Primer pair: Forward 5’-AGCTTGTGCCTGTCCCTGAG-3’, Reverse 5’-GGGCTGGGGAAGAAGGTGT-3’. The sorted cell line, termed J8Zb2m-α-β-, was expanded and maintained in vitro in RPMI + 2 mM L-glutamine + 10% FCS + 100 μg/mL penicillin/streptomycin.

Viral transduction of T-cell lines
SFG-1G4 wild-type and mutant plasmids were synthesized by Genscript. For transfection of the plasmids mentioned above, 293GP cells (Takara Bio, 631458) were co-transfected with 4.5 μg SFG plasmid and 2.25 μg RD114 feline envelope plasmid (provided by S.A. Rosenburg, NIH) using Lipofectamine™ 3000 Transfection Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, L3000075). Viral supernatant was harvested on day 2 post transfection and always used freshly.

T-cell line transduction was mediated by retronectin (Takara, T100B). In brief, retronectin was coated on a non-tissue-culture-treated plate at 10 μg/mL in PBS overnight. Coated plates were washed by PBS and blocked by 2% FBS in PBS for 30 min at room temperature. The blocking solution was aspirated, viral supernatant was added to the coated plates, and the plates were centrifuged at 2500×g for 2 h at 32°C. Viral supernatant was aspirated after centrifugation. Cells were loaded on plates and spun at 300 g for 30 min at 32°C. On day 2 post transduction, transduction rates were measured by flow cytometry (see below) after staining with phycoerythrin-labeled anti-human TCR Vβ13.1 antibody (3% v/v, Biolegend, Cat. # 362410). For the TCRα mutant and matching wild-type controls, cells were stained by iTAg tetramer/APC – HLA-A*02:01 NY-ESO-1 (SLLMWITQC) (5% v/v, MBL, Cat. # TB-M011-2; prior to HLA-tetramer activation assay) or APC anti-human CD3 antibody (5% v/v, Biolegend, 317318; prior to NY-ESO-1 peptide-pulsed COS-7-A2 cell activation assay) and enriched using the EasySep™ Human APC Positive Selection Kit II (Stemcell Technologies, 17661). TCRβ mutants showed high transduction efficiency and were not immuno-enriched (Supplementary Fig. 8e). Data shown in Supplementary Fig. 8c, f are mean +/- standard deviation using biologic triplicates. Raw data are provided in Supplementary Tables 6 and 8.

Flow cytometry
For cell-surface staining, cells were stained with antibodies for 45 min in PBS + 0.5% FBS at 4°C. Cells were washed twice with PBS + 0.5% FBS and flow cytometry data were acquired on an LSR Fortessa X-20 using FACSDIVA v9.2 (BD) and analyzed in FlowJo v10.6.2 (BD). Antibodies used in our surface staining are Brilliant Violet 785™ anti-human CD3 antibody (5% v/v, Biolegend, 317330), and PE anti-human TCR Vβ13.1 antibody (3% v/v, Biolegend, 362410). To visualize HLA binding, iTAg tetramer/APC-HLA-A*02:01 NY-ESO-1 (SLLMWITQC) (5% v/v, MBL, TB-M011-2) was used. Cells were counterstained with the viability reagent LIVE/DEAD Fixable Aqua Dead Cell Stain Kit as per manufacturer’s specifications (0.7% v/v, Thermo Fisher Scientific, L34966). Singlet, live cells were identified for further analysis by a standard gating hierarchy (Supplementary Fig. 8d).

NY-ESO-1–HLA tetramer activation assay
J8Zb2m-α-β- cells with or without transduction were loaded onto 96-well plates (Corning, 353072) at 2e5 cells per 100 μL complete medium in triplicates. Plates were left at room temperature for 20 min and transferred to Incucyte SX1 system (Sartorius) for baseline images at 37°C and 5% CO2. The plate was then removed from Incucyte and loaded with 100 μL of iTAg tetramer/APC-HLA-A*02:01 NY-ESO-1 at 8 μg/mL, 4 μg/mL or 0 μg/mL as designated. Cell Stimulation Cocktail (PMA and ionomycin, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 00-4970-93) was added at 1:1000 as a positive control. Again, the plate was left at room temperature for 20 min and transferred to Incucyte system for imaging at 37°C and 5% CO2. Instrumental setting: 20x objective lens, 9 images per well, 2-h scan interval, using Sartorius Incucyte v2023A. Analysis was done using Incucyte Basic Analysis Software v2023A. Data shown in Supplementary Fig. 8b are mean +/- standard deviation using biologic triplicates. Raw data are provided in Supplementary Table 5. P values were determined by unpaired, two-tailed t-tests using Prism 10 software (GraphPad), and the predetermined significance threshold was P < 0.05.

NY-ESO-1 peptide-pulsed COS-7-A2 activation assay
COS-7-A2 cells were treated with NY-ESO-1(157-165) peptide (customized synthesis, Genscript, purity 96.4%) at designated concentrations at 37°C and 5% CO2 for 1 h and washed twice with PBS. J8Zb2m-α-β- cells were mixed with COS-7-A2 cells at 1:2 ratio or treated with Cell Stimulation Cocktail (PMA and ionomycin, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 00-4970-93) at 1:1000 as positive control. Cells were incubated at 37°C and 5% CO2 for 18 h and NFAT activity (ZsGreen positive rate) was readout by flow cytometry. ZsGreen positivity was gated against the untransduced controls. Data shown in Fig. 7i are mean +/- standard deviation using biologic triplicates. Raw data are provided in Supplementary Table 7. P values were determined by unpaired, two-tailed t-tests without adjustment for multiple comparisons using Prism v10 software (GraphPad) or Excel v16.102 (Microsoft), and the predetermined significance threshold was P < 0.05.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Over the past few decades, many studies have elucidated structural data regarding the TCR–CD3 complex in both unbound and ligand-bound states. However, the mechanism through which ligand binding to the extracellular domains induces TCR conformational change and activation remains enigmatic. In this manuscript, Notti and colleagues seek to address this important question by employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). They present the structures of the unliganded TCR–CD3 complex in detergent micelles and nanodiscs, along with the HLA-bound human TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs. This study identifies two previously unobserved conformations of the unliganded TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs, termed “closed and compacted” conformations. Notably, these appear distinct from the “open and extended” conformations reported in detergent environments. Cross-linking data seem to corroborate the idea that these conformations represent the resting state of an unstimulated TCR–CD3 complex on T cells. Furthermore, the structure of the nanodisc-embedded TCR–CD3 complex bound to HLA showcases significant conformational changes upon ligand binding, adopting an “open and extended” conformation. My major concerns are regarding the map quality of the “closed and compacted” conformations, which exhibit significant preferred orientation that could substantially impact the structural model. Given the authors’ aim to discuss the conformational differences between the resting and activated states, these issues are particularly relevant. 1. The ND-I and ND-II maps appear abnormal (Supplementary Figs. 2c, d), which is also indicated by the 3D FSC analyses of these maps (Supplementary Figs. 2f, h). These analyses suggest severe preferred orientation, with missing orientations parallel to the cell membrane. A representative 2D classification image should be included for further evaluation. 2. The authors claim that much of the density in the ND-I and ND-II maps has an estimated local resolution better than 4 Å, asserting that the maps are of sufficient quality to build models. However, more representative local density maps with the corresponding models are needed to validate this claim. In fact, the deposited model does not satisfactorily match the deposited map. 3. It is important to note that preferred orientation may also lead to the density of cholesterol molecules clustering together. 4. Have the authors considered using graphene oxide or some other detergents to improve preferred orientations? Alternatively, tilting the sample stage could be an effective approach. Overall, while the manuscript presents intriguing findings, addressing these concerns regarding map quality and model validation is essential for supporting the authors’ conclusions.

### Reviewer 2

The authors in this research article solve the cryo-EM structure of the αβTCR-CD3 complex in ligand-free and ligand-bound states in lipid nanodiscs. The structures presented indicate a ‘closed’ structure in the unliganded state and an ‘open’ structure in the liganded pMHC bound state thereby suggesting allosteric conformational changes occurring in the complex upon activation. As an initial result, the authors solve the cryo-EM structure of the αβTCR-CD3 complex in detergent micelles (GDN) which indicated a structure very similar to the previous cryo-EM TCR-CD3 structures obtained in detergents. They subsequently solved the structure in native lipid-like environment using nanodiscs. They obtained 2 distinguishable structures of the complex, both much shorter than the structure obtained with GDN, representing a closed-form conformation. The authors then identify that the compaction of the structure in nanodiscs causes changes in the associated cholesterol molecules and further reveal different TCR-CD3 ectodomain-lipid interactions. To identify the physiological resting state of the complex, the authors engineered disulfide linkages based on the ‘closed’ nanodiscs and ‘open’ detergent-based structures. SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis revealed disulfide linkages based on ‘closed’ nanodiscs structures which meant that the closed conformation is the resting structure of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. Finally, the authors solved the cryo-EM structure of αβTCR-CD3 in complex with single-chain-trimeric-pMHC and identified that pMHC-bound conformation was nearly identical to the detergent-derived αβTCR-CD3 structure, which would represent the ‘open’ active conformation. Further, locking the TCR in the ‘closed’ state using disulfide linkage reduced TCR signaling. Overall, the work presented is extensive with multiple cryo-EM structures of the αβTCR-CD3 complex with some biochemical analysis. However, questions remain about the validity and physiological relevance of the ‘closed’ nanodiscs based conformations. The following concerns must be addressed before considering the manuscript for publication in Nature Communications. Major concerns: 1) An important concern is the physiological relevance of the 2 nanodiscs-based ‘closed’ conformations. There is a concern that the 2 conformations are not due to heterogeneity arising from reconstituting the αβTCR-CD3 complex in nanodiscs. A recent study by Dalal et al., Nature Commun., 2024 found that reconstituting pentameric ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC) in different nanodiscs produces distinct structures by cryo-EM. The study also suggested the use of larger nanodiscs mimics lipid membrane environment better. Based on this, did the authors try different nanodiscs based on size to select the best environment to study the αβTCR-CD3 complex? If so, these results should be discussed. 2) There’s a recent study by Natarajan et al., EMBO Rep., 2024 that studied the in situ cell-surface conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex using photo-crosslinkers. This study determined that there were no significant differences between the cell surface and detergent-purified conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. Further, they identified that there were no large conformational changes in the αβTCR-CD3 structure in the presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. The study, based on information from the current manuscript, attempted to detect changes in crosslinks between TCRα-CD3δ region in the presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. However, they couldn’t infer any conformational changes occurring in this region based on their evidence. The Natarajan et al. study needs to be extensively discussed in the manuscript especially since it was conducted on mammalian cells which is much more physiologically relevant than detergents or nanodiscs. 3) In the result section ‘The unliganded TCR-CD3 is closed and compacted in vivo’, multiple cysteine mutants were created to establish disulfide linkages which were tested by SDS-PAGE analyses and Western blotting. However, these mutants must be tested for viability by using pMHC tetramers and compared to the wild type. In Figure 7, S104C/V182C mutant is tested for NY-ESO-1-MHC-tetramer binding. Similarly, all mutants generated should be tested for its viability. In the same experiment, Western blot analyses were done for identifying disulfide linkages between TCRα and CD3δ. However, the blots were stained only for EGFP which is conjugated with TCRβ. To rule out any artifacts, a construct containing a tag should be conjugated to CD3δto aid in CD3δ-TCRαβ crosslinks detection like the one used in Natarajan et al., EMBO Rep., 2024. 4) In the result section ‘The unliganded TCR-CD3 is closed and compacted in vivo’, SDS-PAGE and Western blot analyses were done to identify crosslinks in the unliganded closed conformation. A similar experiment in the presence of pMHC should be done with the same mutant pairs (G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C and S78C-D77C). TCR αβ-CD3δcrosslinks should be absent in the blots for these mutants as pMHC bound form would lead to an ‘open’ conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. We feel this experiment is crucial to support their overall result and conformation-change hypothesis. 5) As indicated by the authors, in the ND-I and ND-II closed conformations, docking of MHC-II-CD4 complex lead to hindrance with the lipid bilayers. This again brings into question the physiological viability of the nanodiscs-bound complexes. 6) In the result section ‘HLA binding is sufficient to trigger TCR-CD3 conformational change’, the authors use S104C-V182C mutant to lock the TCR in the ‘closed’ conformation which resulted in reduced signaling when compared to the WT upon activation. The reason why the signal was not completely abolished is unclear. Perhaps including multiple mutant pairs - G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C or S78C-D77C along with S104C-V182C could completely lock the TCR in the closed conformation and thereby totally abolish signaling. Minor changes: 1) In line 53, ‘TCR-HLA interaction’ should be ‘TCR-pMHC interaction’. 2) The structure illustration in Figure 1b and the color scheme used is indecipherable.

### Reviewer 5

This study from Notti and colleagues provides structural insights into the inter-subunit conformational relationships that can be assumed in the extracellular and transmembrane domains within TCR-CD3 complexes when solubilized in detergent, or when embedded within artificial membranes after reconstitution within nanodiscs. It makes important additions to the growing library of available cryoEM structures of TCR-CD3 complexes by providing examples embedded within membranes, which are expected to be more physiological than detergent solubilized complexes. Unlike prior detergent-soluble structures, showing the ectodomain of the TCR situated more upright relative to the CD3 heterodimers, the two nanodisc-embedded structures (NDI and NDII) adopt more closed arrangements with the TCR variable regions nearly touching the tops of the CD3 heterodimers. In contrast, nanodisc-embedded TCR-CD3 bound to pHLA adopt a more extended open structure in the ectodomain. The juxtamembrane connecting peptides in the extracellular space, as well as the transmembrane domains of the subunits, also show changes in the unliganded NDI/II conformations relative to the liganded states. Notably, the transmembrane regions of the subunits adopt a splayed relationship in the unliganded state that straightens in the liganded structures, consistent with prior functional data. The authors conclude that the more compact NDI and NDII complexes represent the resting state whereas the open configuration represents a liganded signaling conformation, with changes in the orientation of the constituent subunits in the ectodomain, extracellular juxtamembrane connecting peptides, and transmembrane domains providing a mechanism by which pMHC engagement leads to signaling across the membrane. Experimentally, the study relies largely on cryoEM with some supporting biochemical and functional data: 1. The investigators have the required expertise for the study. The structures appear to be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures. a. The lack of order in some regions creates some problems for insights into allosteric changes for NDI and NDII. 2. The methods indicate that different combinations of constructs were used to purify the TCR-CD3 complexes incorporated into nanodiscs for determination of unliganded structures in NDI and ND2 than were used for the liganded complexes. a. While unlikely, it is formally possible that changes in subunit tags, be they HIS or EGFP or 2A tags left on the subunits, could differentially impact the spatial relationship of the subunits within assembled complexes. What motivated the change in approach is unclear but this caveat should be noted. i. Determination of the structures of the unliganded complexes within the same preparation from which particles were picked and refined for determination of the liganded structures would address this caveat and lend confidence to the approach. The expectation is that the unliganded particles would assume the more closed orientation. ii. Providing the complex construct sequences in the supplemental information would be beneficial to the field. 3. The methods would benefit from better referencing and description of the TCR-HLA paired used and the choice thereof. 4. The manuscript would benefit from an explanation as to why, for the liganded structures, the investigators are confident that the ND-embedded complexes underwent an allosteric change from NDI or NDII. Is there a chance that a subset of complexes existed in an open conformation that favored binding, and that the process of picking and refining particles preferentially enriched liganded particle? 5. The biochemical and functional experiments are performed by conventional techniques, are well-controlled, and are reasonably well-presented for interpretation but they do not add much to the study. a. One caveat is that there is no indication that the disulphide blots or functional assays were performed more than once to ensure reproducibility. b. The methods do not indicate the temperature at which the functional assays were performed (presumably 37ºC). i. This detail is important to ensure others in the field could reproduce the work. c. It would aid in evaluation to add the molecular weights to the blots in Sup Fig 5 rather than color coding the marker and requiring the reader to cross reference the figure legend each time. d. The full gel for Sup Fig 5d and 5e would be helpful for evaluating the extent to which mature complexes are enriched through purification. The zeta subunits are below the cropping of the gel. e. The conclusions regarding Fig 7i and 7j are questionable given the data. i. The histograms in Fig 7i clearly show lower expression of the S104C/V182C mutant than the WT (note that the x-axis is on a log scale). The difference in tetramer staining, as well as the difference in signaling in Fig 7j, could easily be due to differences in surface expression of the WT and mutant TCRs. ii. I recommend removing these data as they do not add to the study and could be misinterpreted. iii. For these data to be convincing, the investigators would need to make multiple independently generated sets of Jurkat lines with matched TCR expression and show that they consistently produced functional differences between the WT and Mut. iv. The investigators should also show that the disulphide bonds are formed on TCR-CD3 complexes that have translocated to the cell surface. Title, Abstract, and Discussion level conclusions: 6. The structures provided herein are interesting and make an important contribution to the field. They provide strong evidence that different inter-subunit conformational relationships can be adopted by the transmembrane and connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3 complex subunits. That alone is important information for the field. 7. The title and abstract level conclusions cannot fully be substantiated by the data and should be calibrated to better reflect the limitations of the data. a. The conclusion that the more closed NDI/II structures represent the resting state are one of several plausible interpretations of the data. As the authors note, the T cell membrane has variable subdomains with different lipid compositions, and it is unclear if porcine neuron membranes are analogous to the membrane subdomain inhabited by TCR-CD3 complexes on the T cell membrane. b. Different environments will have different membrane curvatures (e.g., during transport to the cell membrane or when localized at the tip of a filapodia). Given that the complex is membrane-anchored during assembly and transport to the cell surface, the different conformations may represent assembly or vesicular transport conformations necessitated by the nature of those membrane. c. The effort to present functional data in Fig 7 to support their conclusions is not convincing for the reasons outlined above. These data should be removed. 8. The Discussion level conclusion “…that intrinsic conformational change in the TCR-CD3 is necessary for early TCR-CD3 activation” is not fully substantiated by the data for the reasons outlined above. However, discussing the structures presented here within the context of biochemical and functional data from other studies that support their interpretation would allow the authors to offer a plausible molecular mechanism for those prior observations and lend confidence to the author’s contention that intrinsic changes within the complex occur in the absence of intracellular kinase signaling. a. In addition to the paper cited by the authors (PMID: 34260912), it would be relevant to discuss studies showing exposure of cytoplasmic juxtamembrane proline rich sequence on CD3e can occur in the absence of kinase signaling (even at 4ºC) (PMID: 12110186, 15728235). b. Data that more directly complements the ligand-induced transmembrane allosteric changes observed here, and which should also be noted for completeness, comes from a study indicating that the zeta transmembrane domains are splayed in TCR-CD3 in the resting state and move together in the liganded state in the absence of intracellular signaling (PMID: 26231119). 9. The discussion regarding the potential role of glycosylation in regulating signaling is interesting. a. There is evidence for regulation of gdTCR-CD3 through differential glycosylation that may be worth considering (PMID: 12438426). 10. Evidence that TCR-CD3 inhabits specific membrane sub-domains that concatenate with other distinct sub-domains (e.g., LAT containing domains) are worth consideration (PMID: 20010844). If distinct membrane sub-domains have distinct thicknesses and composition, this could force changes in intra- and inter-subunit transmembrane orientations. They could also exchange sterols at the subdomain interface. They could also potentially impact lipid-protein interactions at the conserved patches noted on CD3. Regarding novelty, extensibility, broad interest and overall impact: 11. This study highlights the value of determining the structures of multi-subunit complex in the membrane environment . a. Doing so for the TCR-CD3 complex is highly novel. 12. This study provides key evidence that inter-subunit allosteric changes in the transmembrane and juxtamembrane extracellular connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3 complex can occur upon ligand engagement. a. This finding is not novel in the broad sense that evidence already exists for allosteric changes in TCR-CD3 upon ligand engagement in the absence of other signaling events, as noted above; nevertheless, it offers important molecular insights into how these changes could occur. b. A key strength of this study, for which it should make an important impact on the field, is therefore derived from contributing to a growing body of evidence that such conformational changes are the earliest events in TCR-CD3 signaling upon engagement of cognate ligands. 13. This study is likely to be of broad interests to people who study multi-subunit signaling receptors, lymphocyte activation, and receptor biology more broadly. 14. This study will also be of impact for its extensibility. The author’s present many key findings that are idea generating, and these ideas are worth testing to work towards a better understanding of this complex.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Notti et al. Response to Reviewer Comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Over the past few decades, many studies have elucidated structural data regarding the
TCR–CD3 complex in both unbound and ligand-bound states. However, the mechanism
through which ligand binding to the extracellular domains induces TCR conformational
change and activation remains enigmatic. In this manuscript, Notti and colleagues seek
to address this important question by employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
They present the structures of the unliganded TCR–CD3 complex in detergent micelles
and nanodiscs, along with the HLA-bound human TCR–CD3 complex in nanodiscs.
This study identifies two previously unobserved conformations of the unliganded TCR–
CD3 complex in nanodiscs, termed “closed and compacted” conformations. Notably,
these appear distinct from the “open and extended” conformations reported in detergent
environments. Cross-linking data seem to corroborate the idea that these conformations
represent the resting state of an unstimulated TCR–CD3 complex on T cells.
Furthermore, the structure of the nanodisc-embedded TCR–CD3 complex bound to
HLA showcases significant conformational changes upon ligand binding, adopting an
“open and extended” conformation.
My major concerns are regarding the map quality of the “closed and compacted”
conformations, which exhibit significant preferred orientation that could substantially
impact the structural model. Given the authors’ aim to discuss the conformational
differences between the resting and activated states, these issues are particularly
relevant.
1. The ND-I and ND-II maps appear abnormal (Supplementary Figs. 2c, d), which is
also indicated by the 3D FSC analyses of these maps (Supplementary Figs. 2f, h).
These analyses suggest severe preferred orientation, with missing orientations parallel
to the cell membrane. A representative 2D classification image should be included for
further evaluation.
Authors’ response:
We thank the referee for reviewing the maps and models. As we described in main text
lines 121-128 and showed in Supplementary Fig. 2f,h, preferred particle orientation and
its effect on 3D reconstruction (i.e., map anisotropy) likely impacted reconstruction
quality, alongside other factors like conformational dynamism. However, efforts to
ameliorate particle orientation preference with graphene oxide grids or fluorinated
detergents did not improve map quality (lines 125-126). Examination of 2D classes for
the nanodisc dataset do show a preference for “top” (membrane normal) views, but
views off this axis are also seen, including views orthogonal or near-orthogonal to the
top view. These data are now included as Supplementary Fig. 2i. Comparison of these
“(tilted)-side” views with those from the GDN dataset (Supplementary Fig. 2j) clearly
show differences corresponding to opening-closing and extension-compaction.
Reviewer #1:
2. The authors claim that much of the density in the ND-I and ND-II maps has an
estimated local resolution better than 4 Å, asserting that the maps are of sufficient
quality to build models. However, more representative local density maps with the
corresponding models are needed to validate this claim. In fact, the deposited model
does not satisfactorily match the deposited map.
Authors’ response:
We refer the reviewer to Supplementary Fig. 3, where the fit of the models to
DeepEMhancer-sharpened maps is shown at the level of whole-density slices (panels c-
e) and zoomed in to areas of interest with specific features serving as intrinsic fiducial
markers across maps (panels f-h). Additional sections through the density maps with
the corresponding models have been added as requested (Supplementary Fig. 3i-k).
We also refer the reviewer to Supplementary Table 2, where model validation statistics
are shown, and highlight that holistic metrics of model quality (e.g., Molprobity score)
and fit (e.g., dFSCmodel) at the standard 0.143 cutoff are in general agreement with (or
in some cases exceed) the nominal resolutions.
To be as transparent and reproducible as possible, we chose the raw,
unsharpened maps to serve as the “primary” maps in the PDB/EMDB, because we
conservatively performed all statistical analyses of map-to-model correlation using these
maps. However, we did also deposit standard global B-factor-sharpened and
DeepEMhancer-sharpened maps in the unified PDB/EMDB deposition system, and
these maps can be accessed in the EMDB (Additional maps 1 and 2 under the
“Additional data” tab for each dataset). For ease of review, we are also uploading all
sharpened maps and the corresponding models to Figshare. We recommend the use of
these sharpened maps for visual inspection, as is standard in single-particle cryo-EM
(see also Methods section, lines 879-888 for a description of map assessment and post
processing). We do note the assessment of reviewer #5, that “[t]he structures appear to
be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that
could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures.”
Lastly, the effect of conformational dynamics on local map quality and its
functional implications merits brief discussion. The local resolution maps for ND-I and
ND-II are consistent with specific regions of disorder and other regions that are well
ordered, suggesting significant conformational dynamics. This interpretation is
consistent with the observation of more than one conformational state (ND-I and ND-II)
within this dataset. The ordering of previously disordered or poorly ordered domains
upon ligand binding is consistent with prior studies showing that ligand binding induces
TCR rigidification (see main text lines 346-351) and suggests that these disorder-to-
order transitions are functionally important. Moreover, the in vivo crosslinking data
presented here (and that of the Krogsgaard group, discussed below) provide support for
the nanodisc conformations as the true physiologic resting state for the TCR.
Taken together, we interpret our ND-I and ND-II maps not as “abnormal,” but as more
biologically accurate reflections of the TCR–CD3’s dynamic resting conformation, which
is reflected in areas of lower local resolution in these maps.
Reviewer #1:
3. It is important to note that preferred orientation may also lead to the density of

Authors’ response:
While map anisotropy might cause “smearing” or “stretching” of the density along axes
perpendicular to missing views, this would not affect solely the density attributed to
cholesterol, and well-ordered regions of the sharpened maps (e.g., ectodomain
immunoglobulin folds) do not suggest a global compression of the reconstruction along

Reviewer #1:
4. Have the authors considered using graphene oxide or some other detergents to
improve preferred orientations? Alternatively, tilting the sample stage could be an
effective approach.
Authors’ response:
Please see main text lines 125-126 for discussion of these efforts. We note also that
DeepEMhancer post-processing has been shown to reduce map anisotropy (Sanchez-
Garcia et al., 2024, PMID: 38612769), which may in part explain the improvement in
map interpretability with application of this post-processing strategy. We have also
tested a recently developed deconvolution-based algorithm for reduction of map
anisotropy (AR-Decon; Li et al., 2025; PMID: 40060637), but this algorithm did not
improve map interpretability or map-to-model correlation, nor did it meaningfully change
the models built from the maps. Indeed, the RMSD between models refined on the
unsharpened maps and the AR-Decon-processed maps were less than 1 Å. As there
are no discernible changes in the models, we do not include these data.
Reviewer #1:
Overall, while the manuscript presents intriguing findings, addressing these concerns

conclusions.
Authors’ response:
See comments above.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors in this research article solve the cryo-EM structure of the αβTCR-CD3
complex in ligand-free and ligand-bound states in lipid nanodiscs. The structures
presented indicate a ‘closed’ structure in the unliganded state and an ‘open’ structure in
the liganded pMHC bound state thereby suggesting allosteric conformational changes
occurring in the complex upon activation.
As an initial result, the authors solve the cryo-EM structure of the αβTCR-CD3 complex
in detergent micelles (GDN) which indicated a structure very similar to the previous
cryo-EM TCR-CD3 structures obtained in detergents. They subsequently solved the
structure in native lipid-like environment using nanodiscs. They obtained 2
distinguishable structures of the complex, both much shorter than the structure obtained
with GDN, representing a closed-form conformation. The authors then identify that the
compaction of the structure in nanodiscs causes changes in the associated cholesterol
molecules and further reveal different TCR-CD3 ectodomain-lipid interactions. To
identify the physiological resting state of the complex, the authors engineered disulfide
linkages based on the ‘closed’ nanodiscs and ‘open’ detergent-based structures. SDS-
PAGE and Western blot analysis revealed disulfide linkages based on ‘closed’
nanodiscs structures which meant that the closed conformation is the resting structure
of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. Finally, the authors solved the cryo-EM structure of
αβTCR-CD3 in complex with single-chain-trimeric-pMHC and identified that pMHC-
bound conformation was nearly identical to the detergent-derived αβTCR-CD3 structure,
which would represent the ‘open’ active conformation. Further, locking the TCR in the
‘closed’ state using disulfide linkage reduced TCR signaling.
Overall, the work presented is extensive with multiple cryo-EM structures of the αβTCR-
CD3 complex with some biochemical analysis. However, questions remain about the
validity and physiological relevance of the ‘closed’ nanodiscs based conformations. The
following concerns must be addressed before considering the manuscript for publication
in Nature Communications.
Major concerns:
1) An important concern is the physiological relevance of the 2 nanodiscs-based
‘closed’ conformations. There is a concern that the 2 conformations are not due to
heterogeneity arising from reconstituting the αβTCR-CD3 complex in nanodiscs. A
recent study by Dalal et al., Nature Commun., 2024 found that reconstituting pentameric
ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC) in different nanodiscs produces distinct structures by
cryo-EM. The study also suggested the use of larger nanodiscs mimics lipid membrane
environment better. Based on this, did the authors try different nanodiscs based on size
to select the best environment to study the αβTCR-CD3 complex? If so, these results
should be discussed.
Authors’ response:
When reconstituting an integral membrane protein in lipid nanodiscs, it is important to
ensure that the MSP size (and thus nanodisc diameter) is sufficient to allow for
incorporation of the membrane with a buffer layer of lipids to minimize obligate MSP-
target protein interactions. The most likely explanation for the different structures
observed for pLGIC in different nanodiscs is that some of the nanodiscs used were too
small in this regard (Hiotis et al., 2025; PMID: 40203538). However, for single-particle
cryo-EM of relatively small membrane protein complexes like the TCR–CD3, it is
necessary to use the smallest possible nanodisc to facilitate particle alignment on
ordered protein density (and not MSP/lipid amorphous density). In this work, we used
the MSP1D1ΔH5 nanodisc system. The referee seems to question whether this
nanodisc might introduce artifacts by being too small for the system of interest. If this
nanodisc were too small, we would expect the TCR to favor an open/extended
conformation, by virtue of insufficient lipid-protein interaction area to promote
compaction and by favoring the smaller TM cross-sectional profile of this “less splayed”
conformation. That is to say, we would expect an inadequately sized nanodisc to
generate an artifactually open/extended TCR–CD3, not to induce the novel
conformations we report here. Nonetheless, prior to pursuing single-particle cryo-EM,
we did simulate the incorporation of the open/extended conformation of the TCR–CD3
(PDB 6JXR at the time) into various sized nanodiscs using the CharmmGUI molecular
dynamics preparation interface. This approach reassured us that the MSP1D1ΔH5
nanodisc ( ~8nm diameter) would have adequate cross-sectional area to incorporate the
only known conformation of the TCR–CD3 at that time with a buffer of lipids between
target protein and MSP. We show these data in Supplementary Fig. 2k-m, and briefly
discuss this in main text lines 117-120.
Reviewer #2:
2) There’s a recent study by Natarajan et al., EMBO Rep., 2024 that studied the in situ
cell-surface conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex using photo-crosslinkers. This
study determined that there were no significant differences between the cell surface and
detergent-purified conformation of the αβTCR-CD3 complex. Further, they identified that
there were no large conformational changes in the αβTCR-CD3 structure in the
presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. The study, based on information from the
current manuscript, attempted to detect changes in crosslinks between TCRα-CD3δ
region in the presence and absence of pMHC tetramers. However, they couldn’t infer
any conformational changes occurring in this region based on their evidence. The
Natarajan et al. study needs to be extensively discussed in the manuscript especially
since it was conducted on mammalian cells which is much more physiologically relevant
than detergents or nanodiscs.
Authors’ response:
We thank the referees for encouraging discussion of this recent work from Michelle
Krogsgaard’s group, which was published during revisions of this manuscript. We make
several points in response to their assessment, and as requested, discuss their findings
extensively in the main text (lines 441-497).
First, we point out that our engineered disulfide crosslinking studies of the human
1G4 TCR (Figure 5) and functional studies in T cells (Figure 7) were indeed performed
in human cells. Natarajan et al. studied the heterologous expression of mouse 2B4 TCR
in human cells, and while the impact of this mismatch on a nuanced understanding of
TCR conformational dynamics is uncertain, our studies of a human TCR in human cells
are at least as physiologically relevant.
Nonetheless, we find that our novel resting state structures are in remarkable
agreement with the data of Natarajan et al., explaining nearly all of their crosslinking
findings for the unliganded TCR–CD3 in situ that they could not explain with the
structures of the TCR–CD3 in detergent. For example, Natarajan et al. report an
unexpected crosslink between the mouse TCRβ CC’ loop residues S170 and G171
(human S186 and G187) and CD3δ. In our models, compaction of the TCR–CD3 in
conformation ND-I brings CD3δ residues 26-30 in closer proximity to TCRβ residues
186 and 187 than the GDN conformation (red arrows, Supplementary Fig. 9a), making
crosslinking plausible. Similarly, Natarajan et al. report crosslinks between the TCRβ
FG-loop and CD3γ, which would not be predicted by the conformation of the TCR–CD3
in detergent (Supplementary Fig. 9b, right). However, closure and compaction in ND-I
bring the FG-loop into close proximity with the CD3γ amino terminus (Supplementary
Fig. 9b, left, dashed circle). Lastly, they report crosslinks between the helix 4–F-strand
region of TCRβ and CD3ϵ and CD3δ, which they wrote could not be explained by the
structure of the TCR–CD3 in detergent. The mouse TCRβ R207 (human R223)
crosslink to CD3ϵ is indeed incompatible with the GDN conformation (Supplementary
Fig. 9c, right), but this residue is brought into close proximity of CD3ϵ in the ND-I
conformation (Supplementary Fig. 9c, left). In contrast to their assessment, the mouse
TCRβ F202 (human F218) crosslink to CD3δ is compatible with both the open/extended
and ND-II closed/compacted conformations that we report (Supplementary Fig. 9d).
Taken together, the photo-crosslinking data reported by Natarajan et al. provide strong
in vivo support for our novel, closed/compacted resting conformation for the TCR–CD3
complex.
Natarajan et al. went on to analyze the effect of activating ligands (pMHC
tetramers and activating antibodies) on TCR–CD3 conformation using their photo-
crosslinking assay. However, we contend that this analysis was flawed in the following
ways and cannot exclude the possibility of ligand-induced conformational change:
1. Most p-azido phenylalanine substitution sites used in this study would not be
expected to show changes in subunit-level crosslinking pattern on ligand-induced
receptor activation. In Figure 6a of their report, Natarajan et al. schematize the
sites selected for crosslinking readout with and without activating ligands. Most of
these sites (exceptions discussed below) are at the core interfaces between the
CD3 ectodomains and/or the TCR constant domains. Our models do not suggest
that there are gross structural changes at these interfaces, and thus we would
not predict changes in crosslinking readout from these mutants.
2. We might have hypothesized that changes in the FG-loop-directed crosslinks
would be observed on ligand binding (TCRβ E221, W225 in their study).
However, the only ligand used to stimulate the receptor for these mutants was
the FG-loop-binding H57 antibody, and by our read of the report, it is not
apparent that binding of the antibody to the mutants was assessed. For example,
the side chain of W225 stabilizes the fold of the FG-loop, forming the
hydrophobic core of this microdomain. Mutation of this residue would be
reasonably expected to affect H57 binding. Lastly, without quantitation, it is
difficult to assess whether the reporters are not in fact showing any changes in
crosslinking efficiency.
3. Natarajan et al. directly assessed crosslinks based on our reported TCRα and
CD3δ interface and their crosslink-based computational models. One crosslink
designed from each of these structural hypotheses was expressed on the cell
surface. The reporter based on our cryo-EM models formed a crosslink between
TCRα and CD3δ (see their Appendix Fig. 16c) and the reporter based on their
open/extended model did not form a crosslink. As with the other crosslinking data
discussed above, this finding actually supports our novel resting state
conformations.
4. They show that qualitatively, this crosslink (human CD3δ D77 p-Aza to TCRα)
persists after activating ligand exposure. However, this is what we would expect
given the low structural resolution and nonspecificity of the photocrosslinking
approach. That is to say, the crosslinking readout in their report is unidirectionally
specific: while the p-azido phenylalanine mutation site is specified, the site of
crosslinking on the target polypeptide is not. A complex in two different
conformations for which the photocrosslinker remains in close proximity to the
target polypeptide chain (even in proximity of totally different target residues) will
still show a crosslink-induced gel shift on Western blot by this assay. For both of
our open/extended conformations (GDN and ND-HLA), the D77 Cβ remains 8-9
Å from TCRα (Supplementary Fig. 9e). This distance is comparable to the 9-10 Å
radius previously used by the Krogsgaard group as a cutoff for plausible
crosslinking (Wang et al., 2014; PMID: 25061810). Modeling the UV-activated
nitrene intermediate of CD3δ D77 p-azido phenylalanine into ND-HLA as the
most likely rotamer of tyrosine places the reactive nitrene less than 4 Å from the
TCRα backbone (Supplementary Fig. 9e).
3) In the result section ‘The unliganded TCR-CD3 is closed and compacted in vivo’,
multiple cysteine mutants were created to establish disulfide linkages which were tested
by SDS-PAGE analyses and Western blotting. However, these mutants must be tested
for viability by using pMHC tetramers and compared to the wild type. In Figure 7,
S104C/V182C mutant is tested for NY-ESO-1-MHC-tetramer binding. Similarly, all
mutants generated should be tested for its viability.
Authors’ response:
The hypothesis being tested by these crosslinking experiments was structural, not
functional. HLA binding is not germane to the question here, which is strictly whether
the residues are present within a specified radius of one another. We make no assertion
of the HLA-binding competence of these mutants, with the exception of that used for
functional analyses (TCRα S104C/V182C).

It is not clear what specific artifacts are hypothesized by the referee. For each of the
