Unfortunately, the proposed experiment is not compatible with the engineered disulfide
system. The disulfides form on exposure to molecular oxygen during complex
assembly. Their formation is not temporally controlled.
We reiterate that the role of the engineered disulfide experiments was to test
whether the conformation of the unliganded TCR–CD3 in the cellular context is
empirically consistent with the observed conformation in nanodiscs or with that in
detergents. The ligand-bound conformation was then observed directly in nanodiscs
and is consistent with the ligand-bound form observed in detergents. We do not
hypothesize that the ligand-bound form in vivo would be distinct from that observed in
these two separate structural model systems. To reiterate, the point of this experiment
was to settle a conflict of physiological relevance between structural models from two
different systems, and no such conflict exists for the ligand-bound conformation.
Reviewer #2:
5) As indicated by the authors, in the ND-I and ND-II closed conformations, docking of
MHC-II-CD4 complex lead to hindrance with the lipid bilayers. This again brings into
question the physiological viability of the nanodiscs-bound complexes.
Authors’ response:
We disagree with the referee’s interpretation of these modeling results. We predict that
our ND-I and ND-II conformations are permissive for HLA binding by computational
modeling, and when we mix unliganded TCR in nanodiscs with HLA we indeed observe
complex formation (see ND-HLA structure). HLA binding to TCR–CD3 triggers a
conformational change into the open/extended conformation. We show by modeling that
the geometry of this conformation is permissive of TCR-pHLA-coreceptor ternary
complex formation. These results are entirely consistent with a model in which HLA
binds to the TCR, inducing a conformational change, which then permits ternary
complex formation and signal transduction.
Referee #2:
6) In the result section ‘HLA binding is sufficient to trigger TCR-CD3 conformational
change’, the authors use S104C-V182C mutant to lock the TCR in the ‘closed’
conformation which resulted in reduced signaling when compared to the WT upon
activation. The reason why the signal was not completely abolished is unclear. Perhaps
including multiple mutant pairs - G79C-D77C, G79C-N38C or S78C-D77C along with
S104C-V182C could completely lock the TCR in the closed conformation and thereby
totally abolish signaling.
Authors’ response:
While we agree that testing multiple pairs is indeed interesting and ongoing work will
address similar questions, this work is outside the scope of the current manuscript. We
show here a single engineered disulfide mutant pair with surface expression and ligand
binding comparable to wild type to avoid confounding from impaired surface expression
and/or receptor affinity. Identifying double or even triple engineered disulfides that do
not compromise these functions is likely to prove challenging. (As it stands, Reviewer
#5 finds even the single mutant’s surface expression to be unacceptable.)
There are several possible reasons for the partial amelioration of signaling. The
disulfide may not form reliably in 100% of cell surface-localized receptors, resulting in a
mixed population on the cell surface. Even if formed, the disulfide may not completely
prevent conformational change, perhaps allowing formation of intermediate
conformations, if not the open/extended conformation, per se. Lastly, ligand-induced
clustering may otherwise change the membrane milieu in ways that “tip the scales” to
allow for partial (suboptimal) signaling even without conformational change. None of
these hypothetical caveats are mutually exclusive. Nonetheless, the ability of this
mutant to reduce peak signaling with surface expression and ligand binding grossly
comparable to wild type is evidence of the importance of conformational change in the
process of ligand-induced receptor activation. We now discuss these caveats explicitly
in the text (lines 498-510).

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
This study from Notti and colleagues provides structural insights into the inter-subunit
conformational relationships that can be assumed in the extracellular and
transmembrane domains within TCR-CD3 complexes when solubilized in detergent, or
when embedded within artificial membranes after reconstitution within nanodiscs. It
makes important additions to the growing library of available cryoEM structures of TCR-
CD3 complexes by providing examples embedded within membranes, which are
expected to be more physiological than detergent solubilized complexes. Unlike prior
detergent-soluble structures, showing the ectodomain of the TCR situated more upright
relative to the CD3 heterodimers, the two nanodisc-embedded structures (NDI and
NDII) adopt more closed arrangements with the TCR variable regions nearly touching
the tops of the CD3 heterodimers. In contrast, nanodisc-embedded TCR-CD3 bound to
pHLA adopt a more extended open structure in the ectodomain. The juxtamembrane
connecting peptides in the extracellular space, as well as the transmembrane domains
of the subunits, also show changes in the unliganded NDI/II conformations relative to
the liganded states. Notably, the transmembrane regions of the subunits adopt a
splayed relationship in the unliganded state that straightens in the liganded structures,
consistent with prior functional data. The authors conclude that the more compact NDI
and NDII complexes represent the resting state whereas the open configuration
represents a liganded signaling conformation, with changes in the orientation of the
constituent subunits in the ectodomain, extracellular juxtamembrane connecting
peptides, and transmembrane domains providing a mechanism by which pMHC
engagement leads to signaling across the membrane.
Experimentally, the study relies largely on cryoEM with some supporting biochemical
and functional data:
1. The investigators have the required expertise for the study. The structures appear to
be reasonably presented and interpreted given the maps, which highlight residues that
could not be built for the NDI and NDII structures.
a. The lack of order in some regions creates some problems for insights into allosteric
changes for NDI and NDII.
Authors’ response:
We thank the reviewer for their careful and thoughtful analysis of the paper. As they
point out, we were conservative in our modeling of the structure, omitting regions where
disorder prevents reasonable modeling of protein backbone, sidechain, glycan, or lipid
atoms. Disorder-to-order transitions are functionally important and ubiquitous
throughout protein biochemistry. While such a transition precludes confident modeling
of disordered residues in static structures, that does not, in our view, detract from their
functional significance. Much in the way that allostery might be explained
mechanistically through a transition between two well-ordered states, it can also be
explained mechanistically through a disorder-to-order transition. Our data are in
agreement with the data reported by others showing rigidification of the TCR upon
ligand binding (references 15 and 32 in main text), suggesting this disorder-to-
order transition is mechanistically important for early TCR activation.
Reviewer #5:
2. The methods indicate that different combinations of constructs were used to purify
the TCR-CD3 complexes incorporated into nanodiscs for determination of unliganded
structures in NDI and ND2 than were used for the liganded complexes.
a. While unlikely, it is formally possible that changes in subunit tags, be they HIS or
EGFP or 2A tags left on the subunits, could differentially impact the spatial relationship
of the subunits within assembled complexes. What motivated the change in approach is
unclear but this caveat should be noted.
Authors’ response:
We agree that differences in carboxy-terminal tags are highly unlikely to explain
differences in conformation of the complex, given that the carboxy-termini of the TCR–
CD3 constituents are unstructured and thus not observed in the cryo-EM maps. When
we began this work, it was anticipated that tandem affinity purification would be needed
to obtain intact complex. This was fortunately not the case, and we thus simplified our
constructs during the course of this investigation. Nonetheless, the position of the His
tag is the same in all constructs used for cryo-EM, all constructs use furin cleavage site-
P2A linkers between complex components on the same virus, and all constructs have a
carboxy-terminal fluorescent protein fusion to TCRβ. In the three-virus expression
scheme, CD3ζ carries a carboxy-terminal EGFP fusion, which is separated from the
structured components by over 100 disordered amino acids; therefore, we think it
exceedingly unlikely that this would affect the structural models we report. Indeed, the
crosslinking studies were performed without a carboxy-terminal EGFP fusion on CD3ζ
and are consistent with the cryo-EM data. The rationale for vector simplification is now
noted in the text, lines 672-675.
Reviewer #5:
3. The methods would benefit from better referencing and description of the TCR-HLA
paired used and the choice thereof.
Response:
We have added additional references providing the full history of the 1G4(LY) TCR
specific for the NY-ESO-1 cancer-testis antigen.
Reviewer #5:
4. The manuscript would benefit from an explanation as to why, for the liganded
structures, the investigators are confident that the ND-embedded complexes underwent
an allosteric change from NDI or NDII. Is there a chance that a subset of complexes
existed in an open conformation that favored binding, and that the process of picking
and refining particles preferentially enriched liganded particle?
Author’s response:
As discussed in the main text, lines 112-117, we attempted to bias data processing of
the unliganded TCR–CD3 in nanodisc dataset towards identifying the open/extended
conformation, but this did not yield any 3D reconstructions consistent with the
open/extended conformation. Analysis of 2D classification data (now in Supplementary
Fig. 2i,j) shows no classes of particles specifically suggestive of the open/extended
conformation. Despite due diligence to identify an open/extended subset of particles in
the resting state dataset, we do not detect this in our data.

a. One caveat is that there is no indication that the disulphide blots or functional assays

i. This detail is important to ensure others in the field could reproduce the work.

Reviewer #5:
e. The conclusions regarding Fig 7i and 7j are questionable given the data.
i. The histograms in Fig 7i clearly show lower expression of the S104C/V182C mutant
than the WT (note that the x-axis is on a log scale). The difference in tetramer staining,
as well as the difference in signaling in Fig 7j, could easily be due to differences in
surface expression of the WT and mutant TCRs.
ii. I recommend removing these data as they do not add to the study and could be
misinterpreted.
iii. For these data to be convincing, the investigators would need to make multiple
independently generated sets of Jurkat lines with matched TCR expression and show
that they consistently produced functional differences between the WT and Mut.
iv. The investigators should also show that the disulphide bonds are formed on TCR-
CD3 complexes that have translocated to the cell surface.
Authors’ response:
Relative to the untransfected control, surface expression of CD3ϵ, surface expression of
TCRβ, and ligand binding by the mutant are all grossly comparable to the wild type.
Indeed, this mutant-wild type pair compares quite favorably with other published
examples of engineered T-cell panels with purportedly “similar” ligand binding, including
from Nature Communications (e.g., Supplementary Fig. 3C in Finnigan et al., 2024;
PMID: 38459027). Nonetheless, we now show data for independently transduced TCR
clones, for which surface CD3ϵ, surface TCRβ, and HLA-tetramer binding in the TCRα
S104C/V182C mutant is at least numerically equivalent to (if not greater than) the wild
type (Supplementary Figure 8c, Supplementary Table 6). For these clones, we assayed
TCR activation in a more demanding and physiologically relevant system using HLA-
A*02:01-positive COS-7-A2 cells presenting NY-ESO-1 peptide to stimulate the reporter
cells instead of HLA-tetramers. In this more rigorous assay, we observed an even more
pronounced phenotype, with the mutant showing a 42% reduction in activated T cells
(Fig. 7i, Supplementary Table 7). We still include the data from the original clones
assayed with the HLA-tetramer assay, as they are from an independent clone set and
are consistent with these new data in a separate experimental system, but we have
moved them to the Supplement (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Table 5).
Regarding disulfide formation, we demonstrate robust disulfide formation for this
double-cysteine mutation pair by mass spectrometry (Figure 5e and Supplementary
Table 4). Although this analysis does not allow us to quantify the fraction of disulfide-
crosslinked TCRs on the cell surface in the Jurkat model, the mass spectrometry data
from HEK cells make it reasonable to infer that the disulfide is present in some fraction
of surface-expressed receptor complexes. We discuss in the main text the caveats
inherent in disulfide formation efficiency being unquantified.
Reviewer #5:
Title, Abstract, and Discussion level conclusions:
6. The structures provided herein are interesting and make an important contribution to
the field. They provide strong evidence that different inter-subunit conformational
relationships can be adopted by the transmembrane and connecting peptides of the
TCR-CD3 complex subunits. That alone is important information for the field.
7. The title and abstract level conclusions cannot fully be substantiated by the data and
should be calibrated to better reflect the limitations of the data.
a. The conclusion that the more closed NDI/II structures represent the resting state are
one of several plausible interpretations of the data. As the authors note, the T cell
membrane has variable subdomains with different lipid compositions, and it is unclear if
porcine neuron membranes are analogous to the membrane subdomain inhabited by
TCR-CD3 complexes on the T cell membrane.
b. Different environments will have different membrane curvatures (e.g., during
transport to the cell membrane or when localized at the tip of a filapodia). Given that the
complex is membrane-anchored during assembly and transport to the cell surface, the
different conformations may represent assembly or vesicular transport conformations
necessitated by the nature of those membrane.
Author’s response:
We agree that the membrane subdomains within a given cell are numerous, with
diverse physicochemical profiles. To say there is a single “native” membrane
environment, for example, would be overly simplistic. Future efforts are aimed at
determining how these various membrane environments alter TCR structure and
function. However, the data we show here are the first to determine the structure of the
TCR–CD3 complex in a lipid bilayer of any kind and is thus a priori a more plausible
model of the TCR–CD3 than any of the unliganded TCR–CD3 models from detergent,
which have been – and continue to be – published in the highest impact journals without
apparent concern for the physiological relevance of the micellar environment. Our
model is then supported empirically by the engineered disulfide crosslinking data from
human cells (this manuscript) as well as the independently generated photo-crosslinking
data from the Krogsgaard group (see discussion above; Natarajan et al., 2024, EMBO
Reports). Moreover, we show that the TCR–CD3 undergoes large conformational
changes in this model membrane environment in response to activating ligands,
providing further evidence that the ND-I/II conformational family represent a ligand-
receptive resting state. While this model may be nuanced by future studies of
membrane composition and geometry on TCR–CD3 structure and function, we argue
that our interpretation of the data has adequate empiric support and is the most
parsimonious explanation for the data at hand.
c. The effort to present functional data in Fig 7 to support their conclusions is not
convincing for the reasons outlined above. These data should be removed.
Authors’ response:
See above.
Reviewer #5:
8. The Discussion level conclusion “…that intrinsic conformational change in the TCR-
CD3 is necessary for early TCR-CD3 activation” is not fully substantiated by the data for
the reasons outlined above. However, discussing the structures presented here within
the context of biochemical and functional data from other studies that support their
interpretation would allow the authors to offer a plausible molecular mechanism for
those prior observations and lend confidence to the author’s contention that intrinsic
changes within the complex occur in the absence of intracellular kinase signaling.
a. In addition to the paper cited by the authors (PMID: 34260912), it would be relevant
to discuss studies showing exposure of cytoplasmic juxtamembrane proline rich
sequence on CD3e can occur in the absence of kinase signaling (even at 4ºC)(PMID:
12110186, 15728235).
b. Data that more directly complements the ligand-induced transmembrane allosteric
changes observed here, and which should also be noted for completeness, comes from
a study indicating that the zeta transmembrane domains are splayed in TCR-CD3 in the
resting state and move together in the liganded state in the absence of intracellular
signaling (PMID: 26231119).
Authors’ response:
Previous length limitations had unfortunately prevented us from including discussion of
a number of deserving studies from the vast, over four-decades-long TCR literature.
However, we have now been able to include the supplied references, and appreciate
the Reviewer’s assistance in curating these.
Reviewer #5:
9. The discussion regarding the potential role of glycosylation in regulating signaling is
interesting.
a. There is evidence for regulation of gdTCR-CD3 through differential glycosylation that
may be worth considering (PMID: 12438426).
Authors’ response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in the role of glycosylation in regulation of TCR
function. As the γδTCR has notable structural, functional, and biochemical differences
from the αβTCR – including the location of its glycosylation sites – we will
conservatively limit our discussion to the αβTCR for this manuscript.
Reviewer #5:
10. Evidence that TCR-CD3 inhabits specific membrane sub-domains that concatenate
with other distinct sub-domains (e.g., LAT containing domains) are worth consideration
(PMID: 20010844). If distinct membrane sub-domains have distinct thicknesses and
composition, this could force changes in intra- and inter-subunit transmembrane
orientations. They could also exchange sterols at the subdomain interface. They could
also potentially impact lipid-protein interactions at the conserved patches noted on CD3.
Authors’ response:
We agree with the reviewer’s inclination that lipid membrane environment may impact
TCR structure and function, and this work is ongoing, as discussed above.
Reviewer #5:
Regarding novelty, extensibility, broad interest and overall impact:
11. This study highlights the value of determining the structures of multi-subunit
complex in the membrane environment .
a. Doing so for the TCR-CD3 complex is highly novel.
12. This study provides key evidence that inter-subunit allosteric changes in the
transmembrane and juxtamembrane extracellular connecting peptides of the TCR-CD3
complex can occur upon ligand engagement.
a. This finding is not novel in the broad sense that evidence already exists for allosteric
changes in TCR-CD3 upon ligand engagement in the absence of other signaling events,
as noted above; nevertheless, it offers important molecular insights into how these
changes could occur.
b. A key strength of this study, for which it should make an important impact on the field,
is therefore derived from contributing to a growing body of evidence that such
conformational changes are the earliest events in TCR-CD3 signaling upon
engagement of cognate ligands.
13. This study is likely to be of broad interests to people who study multi-subunit
signaling receptors, lymphocyte activation, and receptor biology more broadly.
14. This study will also be of impact for its extensibility. The author’s present many key
findings that are idea generating, and these ideas are worth testing to work towards a
better understanding of this complex.
Authors’ response:
We thank the reviewer for their complementary assessment of our work’s novelty and
implications.
